inline.s: Stupa Inscription for Master Baozang Cheng, Founding Patriarch of Puji Hermitage

Master Baozang, whose Dharma name was Zicheng, was a son of the Liu family of Dezhou in Shandong. In youth he learned the smith’s trade, and there at the hammer and tongs he already made the recitation of the Buddha’s name his work, as the Buddha taught the goldsmith’s method. Thus he set his mind for many years. His father died early and his mother lived in widowhood; by nature he was deeply filial and supported her with all his strength. At thirty he conceived the will to leave the world, and was shaved and dyed under Master Tan of the Bell Tower Monastery in his own province, at once establishing himself in sitting meditation and practicing the gate of calm abiding and insight. He wished to go on pilgrimage, but his mother was old and unprovided for; he therefore set aside his own gear to keep her, and carried her with him as he wandered the four quarters. Whenever he begged food he served his mother beneath trees or among the graves, and wished her long life with such cheer that it was no less than a feast of vessels. Later he came to the Western Hills of the capital, to Baihua Zhongyu, and went to and fro there for several years; the local people honored him and their offerings grew daily more ample, yet beyond a single gourd the master had not one crumb to spare. Thus he saw his mother to the end of her allotted years, cremated her according to the rite, and built a stupa to mark his filial devotion, which still stands. Afterwards he built a hermitage and lived at Yuejiapo in Dayu. The palace eunuch Lord Fu gathered the assembly and asked the master to dwell at Pu’an Monastery in the capital. Before long the lay patron Zhang built Puji Hermitage in Sili Garden outside the Fucheng Gate, to receive travelers from the ten directions. In the eighth month of autumn in the gengxu year of Jiajing the great barbarian host invaded the capital; the enemy pressed three sides of the city without a gap, and the people mostly broke and fled, only the western rampart remaining to be encircled. It happened that the barbarian chieftain led several thousand horsemen galloping up to the head of the hermitage and, watering their horses, settled there insolently. The chieftain suddenly entered the hermitage with his men crowding behind him. The master looked at him with a simple, vacant smile and cursed him, saying, “Barbarian slave, do not lay hands on my things.” The master had beforehand laid out fresh fruit below the steps. The chieftain saw persimmons red as fire and gladly took one to eat. The master cursed him loudly: “That is not to be eaten!” The chieftain thought he was being tricked and forced himself to eat it; it was exceedingly bitter and astringent. The master then snatched the persimmon from him and gave him a pear; the barbarian ate it and found it sweet, and shouted for joy that the man had not deceived him. Biting his finger, he warned his men: “There are people here; do not kill them at random.” Then he planted his command arrow and left. Presently a barbarian chased the son of the Wang family into the hermitage; the man ran and hid beneath the Buddha’s seat. The barbarian spied him out and was about to bring down his blade when the master seized the barbarian with his hand, wrested the blade and threw it to the ground; the man lived after all. After a while the barbarians gradually withdrew. Chan Master Daguan Ke often praised him, saying, “The master opposed the barbarians with his single body, directing and scolding them to their faces; those he saved alive numbered tens of thousands. This is manifesting the body of a great heavenly general in order to teach the Dharma — how could it be merely the strength of one general who breaks the enemy?” A good man of Hangzhou named Shao dreamed that the monastery guardian urged him to make offerings to the master; he gave his heart in refuge and built Maitreya Hermitage to invite the master. The master in daily life gave no thought to his belly; his robe was patched from refuse rags, and beyond one bowl he had nothing. Whenever he received offerings of rice or flour he emptied his bag entirely to relieve the poor. When not a single grain remained he still did not go begging to patrons; he merely blocked his door with bricks and sat facing the wall, enduring hunger. In time those who knew sent him provisions; when the food was gone he blocked the door as before. This became his constant way. Later, when the rebuilding of Pu’an Monastery was completed, the master returned to the monastery and his disciples increased day by day. At first Master Chun applied himself most diligently, yet the master alone made life hard for Chun: in bitter cold and stifling heat, in lowly and degrading tasks, Chun had to put his body first, and hardly one thing in a hundred was approved. No one understood his intent. When the master’s days were drawing to a close he looked round at the assembly and said, “My having Chun is like a tree having a trunk; as for the branches and leaves growing thick, spreading out and giving ample shade — do you understand?” Before long he passed away without illness, on the first day of the second month of the thirty-ninth year of Jiajing. He lived eighty-nine years and had over fifty rains-retreats as a monk. After the master’s passing, Master Chun greatly expanded Pu’an at the time of the late emperor’s deathbed charge. When the present emperor’s holy mother completed Cishou Monastery she invited Master Chun to be abbot and made his disciple Liaoning the substitute monk. After Chun’s death she made his grandson Ben Zai abbot; when Zai retired through illness, his disciple Yuanying inherited the work. The holy and compassionate one also built Ci’en Monastery as a separate retreat for Zai to rest in his old age. The master’s descendants flourished like spreading branches, exactly as he had said. Is this not hidden Heaven bearing witness that virtue is repaid? On a winter day of the jiawu year of Wanli I was sojourning in the royal city, and his grandson Liaojian, together with Zai and others, brought a record and begged me for an inscription. Thereupon I made this inscription:

Heaven favors none by partial love,
yet still befriends the good;
bright and clear it rules above —
can it be called untrue?
What is true does not decay;
this body is not there.
Were there no Such a One,
how could lastingness appear?
It is our master here
who stored up filial care,
left the dust, forsook the world —
his virtue was the base.
Where he answered beings’ needs
his merits were not one;
by skilful means he wrote
these deeds of wonder done.
He woke to the Unborn,
and so he does not die.
Trunk and branches spread and shade —
it came from one small seed.
He shelters gods and men,
his roots a thousand feet;
one stupa towers aloft
through a thousand autumns, ten thousand ages.
Stupa Inscription for Master Wuxia Yu of Cihui Monastery

The master’s Dharma name was Ming Yu, his style Wuxia; he was a son of the Liu family of Longju in Anyue, in western Shu. From birth he cared nothing for managing property; by nature he was stubborn and would not go along with worldly ways. When grown he married a daughter of the Wang family and had three sons. The eldest was clever and deeply filial; though the master loved him at heart, he still made no plans on account of wife and children. In daily life he made the Buddha his business; whenever he made offerings to his two parents he insisted that vegetarian food was the way to fulfill filial duty, and the two elders found their peace in this. The master’s thought was fixed on rising above the dust and leaving the world, and he never set it aside for a moment. When his two parents departed this life he was forty-six; he at once decisively abandoned wife and children and went wandering beyond the world. At that time his eldest son was twelve; he followed at his father’s heels, and they came to Mount Loutou in Bozhou, to the place of the master of Dongyanghai Hermitage, where father and son were both shaved and made novices and received the full precepts, on the fifth day of the fifth month of the third year of Longqing. From then on the master took his eldest son on pilgrimage and trained him in his studies as a disciple; father and son traveled together, wandering ten thousand li, visiting every famous mountain and calling on good teachers. Their austerities were beyond compare: one meal a day at noon, of bran and greens without grain, under trees or among tombs, content wherever they found themselves. From then on, to the end of his life, his ribs never touched a mat. In the early Wanli years he paid homage at Putuo, passed through Jinling, came to the capital, traveled to Mount Wutai, and lodged at the Three Pagodas Monastery, where he venerated the Avatamsaka Sutra, a sutra of six hundred thousand characters, with one bow for each character, and each day and night he would certainly make three thousand prostrations. Thus he went through it three times. In the twelfth year he again came to Bifeng Monastery in the capital and venerated the Lotus Sutra of over sixty thousand characters, one bow to a character, day and night unwearied, going through it twelve times as before. The eldest son, as a novice, grew daily in years and virtue; he attended many lecture halls, studying the Avatamsaka, Lotus, Śūraṅgama, Perfect Enlightenment and Consciousness-Only sutras and treatises, and he was skilled at opening understanding and instructing the untaught, while serving the master ever more carefully. People marveled at the time, saying that such a master and disciple existed; their fame had already stirred those within and beyond. In the seventeenth year the eunuch Wang of the Directorate of Palace Servants and others wished to open a retreat and invite the master’s disciple as a place for spreading the Dharma, and also as a resting place for the master’s old age; they divined a site about two li outside the Fucheng Gate and donated funds to found a monastery for them to live in. When it was finished they petitioned for a name; the Holy Mother approved and granted the name Cihui. The Minister of Rites, Lord Li Tangxuan, recorded the affair. One day the master said to his disciple, “Bound by karma to the Sahā world for seventy-two years, I have drifted into old age and illness. What use is it to stay long? I am going home. You should keep the Dharma in your heart and give rise to no attachment.” Then he stopped eating and recited the Buddha’s name without pause for ten days; his voice rang like a bell and his complexion seemed robust. When his disciple asked about the great matter of birth and death, the master only said, “Hee hee, ha ha; ha ha, hee hee. Not a deluded thought, not true knowing.” After a long while he said, “What do you say it is?” Then he answered for him: “The grain-tax man on Datong Bridge was originally a rice-carrier from the south.” At the point of death he asked for a bath and changed his clothes, sat upright holding his beads, and his recitation grew more urgent and pitiful; then he cried out again and again, “Buddha, Buddha, Buddha! Driving the iron ox backwards, I return to the Buddha Land.” His voice ceased and he passed away. It was the nineteenth day of the first month of the spring of the yiwei year of Wanli. The master was born in the seventh month of the jiashen year of Jiajing; he lived seventy-two years and had twenty-six rains-retreats. On a certain month and day his whole body was enshrined in the stupa at Huangcun. He had one disciple, Zhengui, who is now Dharma Master Cihui. As I was begging in the royal city, dwelling in the Maitreya Pavilion, Gui brought me a record of his conduct and begged me tearfully, Haiyin, to set down his story. The master in life did not know a single character, yet at his departure he was so free and easy — was he not one whose heel-cord had snapped, who went home along the road? Thereupon I made this inscription:

The mechanism of birth and death
hangs on a single opening.
He came well, he went well —
a wooden man wearing a hat.
Father and son in a circle,
form and shadow looking at each other.
In the world and beyond the world,
what interplay is there?
Old Pang of former days
broke up his home and scattered his house;
seen from today,
he seems not to have let go at all.
How much better this master,
who was opaque to a single opening,
stubborn as twisted iron,
who walked straight out of the cage.
Pang would not marry off his daughter;
the master would not abandon his son —
the same intent,
each getting his own advantage.
Seventy-two years,
half monk, half layman.
Today’s manner of leaving
is a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold enough.
One stupa soaring into space,
ever abiding in the ten directions.
Emptiness may perish, the stupa remains;
the dharmakāya is all the more revealed.
Stupa Inscription for Dharma Master Huan, Style Mian’an, of Sanjiao Mountain

Carefully following the record: the master’s Dharma name was Ruhuan, his style Mian’an; he was a son of the Lin family of Putian, and his father was Lin Huan. The master was spirited and unconventional, carrying an uncommon air. In youth he studied the Confucian classics, and at fourteen he was already enrolled among the scholars. There was a Scholar Xia Zhishi in his village who was versed in the Buddhist canon, and the master’s friendship with him was the closest. One day Xia said to the master, “Your lips protrude and your teeth show; this is not the physiognomy of long life.” The master, startled, asked what could be done. Xia said, “I have heard that when one recites the name of Great Being Avalokiteśvara, no prayer goes unanswered; just hold the name and you will see.” The master accordingly took up the recitation and practiced earnestly for two years, and indeed his lips closed together. At nineteen the Japanese pirates raided Fujian, and both his parents died in the fighting. The master wept bitterly and said, “Is human life really like this? Why cling to one’s native place?” He shook out his robes and roamed the rivers and lakes for two years, then entered Mount Lu and called on Great Master Bianrong. Rong asked, “Where is the Virtuous One from, and what has he come for?” The master said, “This young man is from Fujian and has come seeking long life.” Rong said, “Where there is long there must be short; why not learn the Unborn?” “How does one learn the Unborn? I beg the master to instruct me.” Rong said, “Try shaving off hair and beard, putting all conditions to rest, and chewing on a meaningless phrase; when after a long time you find where it lands, then I can speak to you of the Unborn.” The master was at once shaved and dyed and given the name Ruhuan, and stayed with him a while; then he went to Maya Mountain in Qishui to call on the treasury keeper Wuwei, living there three years, and next hid on Doufang Mountain for five more. Then he shouldered his staff and traveled north to the capital, visiting the great teachers and studying under the two Dharma masters Xian and Li, hearing the profound meanings of the sutras; all the elders thought highly of him. Afterwards General Tian of Qishui, seeing the master’s breadth of mind, tried to draw him into worldly affairs. The master laughed and said, “Would a sea dragon consent to enter a ditch?” Then he dragged his staff back to Jiufeng, where monks gathered in crowds, and he would constantly use the Śūraṅgama Sutra to reveal the essentials of mind to the assembly. The Hanlin scholar Lord Guo Zhengyu, in mourning for his mother, called on the master at Jiufeng, and they took great delight in one another. Guo then pressed him: “I observe that those who talk of Chan nowadays are quick to pride themselves on the staff, the shout and the darting of the pivotal phrase as the highest thing, yet when one examines their actual conduct it is of the least account. If so, it would be better to keep the teachings, refine the precepts, leave desire, practice austerities and benefit beings with compassion, as the master does.” The master said, “So it is. But this is not the fault of Chan, it is the fault of those who study Chan. Alas, the farther we are from the sages the more the Dharma gate declines; truly, as you say, it is enough to make one weep.” The master disciplined himself in plain austerity; all his life he had no cravings, and whatever was given him he gave away again. Whenever he went anywhere he had only one bowl and three robes, bare feet in straw sandals. Lord Shen, a provincial judge of Chu, was his closest friend. His disciples wished to secure land for offerings and had a deed drawn up, informing the master that it came from Lord Shen. The master rebuked them sharply: “The field of the mind is not vigorously hoed — why fuss over Squire Shen?” The disciples paid no heed and privately asked Shen. When the master learned of it he dragged his staff away from Jiufeng to Wuqu and rested at Jiyang Monastery, where he sealed himself in retreat and recited the Avatamsaka Sutra for three years. He went to Sanjiao Mountain in Tanzhou, the place where Zongyin, a disciple of Mazu, had opened the mountain; within a few years it was transformed and the Dharma seat flourished greatly. One day the master said to the assembly, “Zhaozhou was still on pilgrimage at eighty — are my soles so lacking in a pair of straw sandals?” He shook his sleeves and went to Mount Kuang, entering Huanglong Monastery, where he stayed to lecture on the Śūraṅgama Sutra. At the end of the second fascicle he said to the assembly, “Let us set that aside for now; I still have a final phrase to discuss with you all.” He then showed signs of illness and after six days announced his end. The assembly asked him to leave a verse. The master said, “In leaving the world there is no verse; a fool seeks the traces of a dream. Space has no face — ask space for a face.” A disciple asked whether his relics might be taken to Qi. The master said, “The Sahā world is heavy with love and suffering; the heaven of the Pure Land is without feeling. What need to cherish an old shadow? Still radiance fills the three thousand worlds.” With these words he passed away, on a certain day of a certain month in the nineteenth year of Wanli. The master was born in the guisi year of Jiajing; he lived fifty-nine years and had over thirty rains-retreats. His disciples cremated him and buried the bone-relics at a certain place on Huanglong Mountain. His disciple Xingquan, by his dying command, went to the Hanlin scholar Guo of Jiangxia to beg a record of his conduct. In the ninth month of autumn of the renchen year of Wanli, through the Hanlin Guo, I was asked to compose a stupa inscription. So following the record I have set out the story, and made this inscription:

The great sea is vast;
its taste is whole in a single drop.
Sāgara holds it in his mouth
and makes of it clouds and rain.
This single drop
is neither within nor without;
rolled into a hair’s tip,
it spreads through sand-like worlds.
Soft rain falls,
and the parched earth is everywhere soaked.
The three grasses and two trees,
sour, sweet, bitter, pungent,
each gain their growth,
sprouting and sending up stems —
unless a thing is rootless,
it has not been laid waste.
It is our master,
a son of Sāgara:
his poison breath assails men,
and whoever touches it dies;
his out-breathed breath becomes cloud,
his drawn-in breath becomes ice;
cold or hot,
he accords with the season and is honored.
He makes his body water
and water his life;
his transformations have no fixed rule,
his coming and going no constancy.
Flowing or resting in the hollow,
meeting conditions he makes them his school.
Were he not like an illusion,
how could he merge with emptiness?
He comes from nowhere,
goes with nothing to cling to;
riding backwards on the yellow dragon,
he trod Three Peaks till they broke.
The waters of Tanzhou,
the clouds of Mount Kuang,
fill the six directions:
this is the master’s whole body.
Dream Wanderings of Elder Hanshan, Volume Thirty
Biography of My Great-Grandfather, the Great Monk Xilin, Left Jueyi of the Nanjing Buddhist Registry and Abbot of the Great Bao’en Monastery

My grand-master’s Dharma name was Yongning, his style Xilin; he was a son of the Guo family of Luhe County. He left home in childhood and took the Venerable Wuxia Yu of Bao’en as his master. By nature he was upright and steady, never speaking or acting carelessly, and while still young he was held in esteem by the assembly. At twenty he began reciting the Diamond Sutra and never stopped until old age. When Emperor Wuzong visited the southern capital and stayed at our monastery, the Minister of Rites worried that no monk was fit to receive the imperial command; those selected all proved unsuitable. Earlier the master and a monk named Huiyuan, styled Donglin, had been inseparable friends; both were tall and powerfully built. Qiao Baiyan, the Minister of War, had long been friendly with the master, and recommended the two. The Minister of Rites was delighted and at once made Yuan Right Jueyi of the Buddhist Registry and the master Supervisor of our monastery. When the imperial party was lodged in the monastery, the next day the emperor ascended the great hall, finished worshipping the Buddha, and after the officials had made their courtesies he commanded that a sutra-chanting service be held and asked for the draft of the petition. The Minister of Rites proposed that a Hanlin scholar be required. My grand-master said, “Buddhist petitions have their own form, and it is proper that monks compose them.” He then recommended Master Yuan, who presented the draft. The emperor read it with pleasure and said, “Does Our house have such a monk?” The Minister of Rites then handed the seal of the Buddhist Registry to Yuan to hold, so that he might conduct the affair. When the emperor came to the pagoda hall he saw a hole in the floor and asked the monk attending there what it was. He answered “a golden well,” and the emperor was displeased. My grand-master knelt and said, “It is an air-hole.” The emperor asked its use. He said, “The Buddha’s relics are enshrined beneath the pagoda; this is left to let air pass.” The emperor’s mood cleared. The rite was held for seven days; Master Yuan led all the ritual at the altar, while the master handled every matter within and without according to the imperial will. When the emperor departed, nothing had been lacking. From this the Minister of Rites esteemed him highly. In the tenth year of Jiajing the assembly elected him abbot of our monastery, to oversee all its affairs. In the twentieth year he was promoted to Right Jueyi of the Registry, and five years later to Left Jueyi. Previously the Buddhadharma had not flourished greatly in Jiangnan; though the master held office, he grieved for the Dharma gate. Whenever he saw monks slighted by the literati he sighed: “Monks do not study, and so they bring disgrace on the teaching and defile the Dharma gate.” He first invited my late master, the monk Yungu, to live in the Tripiṭaka Hall and teach those practicing Chan; only then did people begin to know that there was a Chan school. Some years later my late master left to live in seclusion at Qixia. It happened that my late master Shouyu came south; Lord Lu Wutai, then a secretary in the Ministry of Rites, said to my grand-master, “I have lately met the eminent monk Dharma Master Shouyu, whose exposition is very clear; he should be invited to the monastery to teach the monks.” The master at once invited him with full courtesy to live in the Tripiṭaka Hall, provided regular support, chose several dozen monks, and daily led them himself to hear the lectures. From then on they began to turn toward the Buddhadharma. My late master Yungu was living at Qixia; Lord Lu, visiting Mount She, met him and greatly esteemed him, and wished to restore the place, inviting him to be abbot. He firmly declined, and instead my grand-master recommended Master Shan of Songshan as abbot of Qixia. Thus the teaching ground was restored, the monastery’s estates recovered, a Dharma society opened, and it became a receiving monastery. From then on Chan and Buddhadharma flourished greatly, and people came to know the practice of receiving travelers from the ten directions — all of it raised up by my grand-master’s effort. Previously most monks followed vulgar ways and could not utter a word before gentlemen. The master used to tell the monks that though Chan and the teachings are their proper work, yet to master letters and understand the great principles of loyalty and filial piety one must first enter by way of the Confucian classics. He therefore engaged Confucian teachers to instruct me and some dozen others in the Five Classics, the Four Books, the philosophers and the histories. It is owing to this that I have a rough knowledge of letters, and that once shaved I knew how to listen to lectures and practice Chan — and that Xuelang restored the teaching of a whole age. All of it was due to the master’s compassionate care in raising and teaching us. The master held the seal of the Registry for twenty-five years; all the monasteries obeyed the Dharma with care, and in the affairs of the monastery not a blade of grass or leaf was lightly cast away. He guarded the community as his own eyes, and so the monastery prospered and the Dharma’s fortune flourished. Whenever he led the monks to the hall to pray for the emperor’s long life and saw monks absent through laziness, he would rebuke them sharply: “This hall is a heavenly palace, a Pure Land. If you are so lazy and negligent, the day will come when you cannot obtain even one glimpse of it.” On the last day of the twelfth month of the forty-third year of Jiajing the master gathered his descendants, recounted the course of his life and entrusted them with his final affairs. Stroking my back, he charged them: “I am eighty-three and must be going. The house has many troubles; a single day without an elder makes it hard to hold together. This boy, young as he is, has plenty of judgment. After I am gone, whenever any matter arises, you of the household, great and small, should stand before my image and follow this boy’s decision; then perhaps you may be kept safe.” My young grand-master, Lord Genshan Hou, and all below him assented. On the seventh day of the first month of the following year the master put on his robe and made a tour of the monks’ quarters, thanking all the elders of the monastery. On the tenth he took the Registry seal and waited on the Minister of Rites, asking to retire on grounds of age. The Minister consoled him and would not consent. The master returned and at once sealed up the seal. The next day he showed a slight illness; a doctor was called with medicine. The master said, “I am finished,” and took no medicine. As I attended him in his illness I heard him ceaselessly reciting the Diamond Sutra. At midnight on the fifteenth he had the whole assembly, great and small, gather round to recite the Buddha’s name, and as I held him sitting in my arms he passed away in silence. It was the sixteenth day of the first month of that year. The master had never accumulated anything; his boxes held less than thirty pieces of gold, while the funeral and burial cost more than three hundred, all of it borrowed. After the burial the whole household was at a loss. My young grand-master was anxious and gathered great and small before the master’s image, but no plan emerged. I then took the lead: we inventoried the master’s robes, bowl and belongings, appraised everything of value and used it all to repay the lenders; if it fell short, land would be sold to make up the sum. Once free of debt, food and clothing would be easy. The assembly agreed. A vegetarian feast was set out and all the creditors gathered, each with his note, and they were paid principal with interest. The notes of what was owed were burned in a single night. Thereupon the household was preserved and the descendants did not scatter. My young grand-master then called the master a judge of men. In the second month of that year the abbot’s quarters burned; on the fifteenth day of the second month of the next year the great hall was destroyed by fire. By imperial decree the monastery’s officials, heads and officers — fifteen men — were handed over to the judicial authorities, for the monastery was the court’s own Buddhist hall, everything in it came from the privy purse, and the matter fell under the weightiest statutes, punishable by death. The monks of the whole monastery were terrified and fled. I alone went to the judicial office, saw to their salt, vegetables and gruel, and carried loads back and forth, meanwhile using every means to shield them and contrive their rescue. In the end the sentence was reduced to a fine of prison rations. Thereupon the monastery was at peace, and all thanked and praised the master as one who knew men. The master was born in the guimao year of Chenghua and lived eighty-three years. The present Xilin Hermitage was the retirement retreat he built in his lifetime; his whole body was buried at Zhi’an Monastery. At twelve I was graciously allowed by the master to leave home, and he had me take Master Meizhai Jun as my teacher and study the scriptures; at nineteen I was shaved and dyed. I attended the master for ten years, and though many small details of his conduct I cannot recall, I saw how every day at dawn he recited and dedicated the merit toward the West without ever neglecting it. Whenever I followed at his heels I saw his dignity and uprightness: he would not hitch up his robe as he walked, his face was iron-severe, and one seldom saw him part his lips in a smile. He served my two late masters Yungu and Shouyu as though before great guests, with utmost reverence and full courtesy; even when ordinary monks from other monasteries came to call, he would not receive them unless properly robed and capped. Yet in teaching me and the others to read he was like a loving mother with an infant. Cherishing gratitude for my grandfather’s grace these fifty years and more, I once wrote a detailed record of his conduct in the Eastern Sea, but the draft was lost when I met with disaster. Now I am old, and nine parts in ten are forgotten. Grieving that later descendants will not know whence their forebear came, I set down this rough account to proclaim it to those who come after, so that the elder’s virtue and bearing may be as if present age after age.

The appraisal says: The way of Heaven revolves and rises or falls with the times, and so it is with the way of Dharma. When the Way is about to flourish, one who answers to the True must come in due season to open it — this is no accident. Consider how the Buddhadharma of Jiangnan lay in primitive obscurity, like relics not yet emerged; today the Dharma rain is full and the air of a Buddha land flows everywhere. Who brought this about? My grandsire did not himself carry the Way, yet the Way came about through him. Is his merit not equal to that of a creator?
Biography of My Late Master Yungu

The master’s Dharma name was Fahui, his style Yungu; he was a son of the Huai family of Xushan in Jiashan, born in the gengshen year of Hongzhi. In childhood he aspired to leave the world and took a certain master of Dayun Monastery in his county as teacher, at first studying Yogācāra ritual. The master would often reflect: “Leaving home turns on the great matter of birth and death — why busy oneself over food and clothing?” At nineteen he resolved to travel, and soon went to the ordination platform to receive the full precepts. Hearing of the Tiantai method of Lesser Calm Abiding and Insight, he devoted himself to it with single-minded care. Chan Master Fazhou Ji, who continued the way of Jingshan, was in retreat at Tianning in the prefecture; the master went to consult him and presented his practice. Zhou said, “The essence of calm abiding and insight does not rely on body, mind or breath, but is free within and without. What you practice has fallen into a lesser vehicle — how could that be the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? In learning the Way one must make awakening the mind the chief thing.” The master, in grief and longing, begged for instruction, and Zhou gave him the huatou “Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?” and had him plant his doubt anew. Following his teaching, the master inquired day and night, forgetting sleep and food. One day as he was eating he did not notice that he had finished; suddenly the bowl fell to the ground and he woke with a start, as if from a dream. He again sought instruction from Zhou and received his seal of approval. Reading the Record of the Mirror of the School, he greatly awakened to the purport that all is mind; from then on all the sutras and teachings, and the kōans of the patriarchs, were clear to him as familiar objects in his own house. He then hid his light in the monasteries and buried himself in lowly tasks. One day, reading the Tanjin Collection, he saw the deep resolve of Great Master Mingjiao to protect the Dharma: at first he worshipped Great Being Avalokiteśvara and recited the name a hundred thousand times day and night. The master vowed to follow his practice, and so carried an image of Avalokiteśvara on his head, staying awake all night in bowing and walking, unwearied to the end of his life. At that time the Buddhadharma and Chan way of Jiangnan were wholly unheard of. When the master first came to Jinling he lodged beneath the Vairocana Pavilion at Tianjie and practiced there, and those who saw him called it strange. The late Prince of Wei heard of it and invited him to be supported at Conggui Hermitage in the Western Garden, where the master dwelt and entered samādhi for three days and nights. Not long after, my great-grand-master Xilin, who held the Registry seal and was abbot of Bao’en, went to call on the master and invited him to live in the Tripiṭaka Hall of that monastery. The master sat upright in a niche, never greeting or seeing anyone off, and for three years his foot did not cross the threshold; no one knew of him. It happened that a powerful nobleman came visiting and, seeing the master sitting upright, thought him rude and insulted him. The master dragged his staff away to Qixia on Mount She. Qixia had been founded in the Liang dynasty, when Emperor Wu carved the Thousand Buddha Cliff; successive dynasties had granted lands for its support, but the teaching ground had fallen into ruin, its halls become a lair of tigers and wolves. Loving its deep seclusion, the master cut thatch below the Thousand Buddha Cliff and never showed himself outside the mountain. Once a thief broke in and stole all he had; the man walked all night and at dawn was still not away from the hermitage. People caught him and brought him to the master, who fed him and let him carry off everything. Hearing of this, people were moved and transformed. Lord Lu Wutai, then a secretary of the Ministry of Rites in his first office, was visiting ancient teaching grounds and happened to come to Qixia. Seeing the master’s uncommon bearing, he esteemed him greatly and lodged in the mountain for two nights, wishing to restore the monastery; he asked the master to be abbot, but he firmly declined and recommended Master Shan of Songshan in his place. Shan recovered all the monastery’s former estates, expelled the powerful men who had occupied the buildings, made an abbot’s hall, built a Chan hall, opened a lecture seat and received those who came from the four quarters. The monasteries of Jiangnan began here — and it was the master’s doing. Once the teaching ground was opened and visitors grew many, the master moved to the deepest part of the mountain, a place called Tiankai Cliff, and dwelt alone with his shadow as before. At that time officials and laymen, through Lord Lu’s guidance, mostly came to know of the Chan way, and hearing of the master’s manner they often came to call. With all who came to consult him, at the first meeting the master would ask, “How is your daily affair?” Regardless of rank, monk or lay, once in his room he would throw a cushion on the ground and have them sit upright and look back at their own original face. Sometimes a whole day and night passed without a word. At parting he always urged, “Do not pass the day in vain.” At a second meeting he would ask about the practice since they parted, and whether it was hard or easy. Thus the careless had no answer. His compassion grew more urgent and his severity heavier; though he had no formal establishment, those who saw him shivered at the cliff’s edge. Yet the master embraced all with an equal mind; in receiving people he always spoke softly and in a low voice, with a single plain regard, never showing a harsh look. Officials and scholars took refuge with him in growing numbers. Even those who could not come into the mountain, if they asked to see him, he would go to them, his mind set on guiding them; once a year he went into the city and always stayed at Huiguang Monastery. Whenever he came, the lay assemblies gathered around him as bees around a flower seat, and he looked on all as illusory people, never giving rise to a single thought of discrimination. So those close to him were like infants beside a loving mother. Outside the city he mostly stayed at Pude, and Master Qühe Yue received his teaching. My late grand-master would often invite him into his quarters, sometimes for ten days or a month. In my boyhood I was close to him and served him, and he graciously thought well of me, never wearying of instructing me. When I was nineteen I had no wish to leave home; the master knew it and asked, “Why do you turn your back on your first resolve?” I said, “I am merely weary of the worldliness of it.” The master said, “If you know how to be weary of worldliness, why not learn to be an eminent monk? The eminent monks of old were not treated by emperors as subjects, nor raised by parents as sons; the gods and dragons revered them and they took no delight in it. Take up the Transmission of the Lamp and the Lives of Eminent Monks and read them, and you will know.” I then searched my book chest and found a copy of the Extensive Record of Zhongfeng, and showed it to the master. He said, “Savor this well, and you will know why it is noble to be a monk.” Thereupon I resolved to be shaved and dyed — truly I was opened and developed by the master. It was the jiazi year of Jiajing. In the winter of the bingyin year, grieving that the Chan way had fallen silent, the master gathered fifty-three people and held a sitting meditation period at Tianjie. He strove to pull me into the assembly to practice with them, pointing out the road beyond, and taught me the huatou “Who recites the Buddha’s name?” Only then did I first know that there was a matter of the Chan school. In all the monasteries of the southern capital, those who practiced Chan numbered only four or five. As the master neared old age his compassion grew more urgent. Even to the youngest novice he looked with compassionate eyes and treated him with courtesy; in every movement and bearing he taught them by word and ear, leading them gently on, so that each who saw him felt he was close to him personally. Yet his resolve to protect the Dharma was deep: he did not slight beginners, nor treat with contempt those who had broken the precepts. Monks of the various monasteries were often unruly, and whenever he heard of one who had violated the rules he would go to his rescue without waiting to be asked, always earnest with the authorities. The Dharma is entrusted to kings and ministers as outer protectors, and they should only seek to embody the Buddha’s mind: to insult a monk is to insult the Buddha. Those who heard him all changed countenance and were set at ease, and he never rested until the man was freed. Yet he never let it be known, and so his listeners never found him troublesome; in time all knew it came from a compassion without conditions. When Lord Yuan Liaofan had not yet passed the examinations he consulted the master in the mountain, sitting silently face to face for three days and nights, and the master showed him the purport that all is mind and that destiny is established by oneself. He followed the teaching, as is detailed in his Record of Self-Examination; from this the master’s way grew daily in weight. In the xinwei year of Longqing I took leave of the master to travel north. He admonished me: “The pilgrims of old went out simply to seek clarity in the matter under their own feet. You should consider how one day you will face your parents, teachers and friends. Take care not to waste the money for your straw sandals.” I bowed farewell in tears. In the spring of the renshen year Lord Wu Moquan, Minister of Personnel of Jiahe, Lord Zheng Danquan, Minister of Justice, and Lord Lu Wutai, Minister of the Imperial Stud of Pinghu, with his brother Yuntai, together invited the master to his old mountain. These gentlemen constantly came into his room to ask about the Way, burning incense at every meeting and begging instruction, observing the courtesy of disciples. Chan Master Daguan Ke, together with Minister Lu Pingquan and the Secretariat official Xu Si’an, once called on the master to inquire into the essentials of the Avatamsaka; the master expounded the wonder of the perfect fusion of the four dharma realms, and all sighed that they had never heard its like. In instructing people the master especially revealed the gate of the mind-only Pure Land. All his life he let things take their course and never set up a formal house of his own; whenever a monastery had a Chan or lecture ground it would invite him to sit in the abbot’s hall, and there he would uphold Baizhang’s rules, insisting on making clear the model of the former worthies without the least indulgence. In daily life he was calm, weighty and sparing of words; when he spoke it was like an echo in an empty valley. Sustained by the power of samādhi, he lived in the mountains in pure practice for over forty years as one day, his ribs never touching a mat, bowing and reciting to the end of his life without missing a single night. In a time when the Chan way of Jiangnan was still in the dark, and moving in and out of places full of talk, he was from first to last without a critic — his conduct can be known from this. The master lived in his home district for three years, and those he transformed by his grace numbered in the thousands and tens of thousands. One night people of the four villages saw a great fire blaze up from his hermitage; when they hurried to look at dawn, the master had quietly passed away. It was the fifth day of the first month of the yihai year, the third of Wanli. He was born in the gengshen year of Hongzhi, lived seventy-five years and had fifty rains-retreats; his disciple Zhenyin and the others cremated him and buried him to the right of the monastery. Since leaving the master I have traveled everywhere and consulted many teachers, but I have not seen one whose conduct was so plain and solid, whose true compassion and serenity were like his. Whenever I think of him, his voice and countenance appear vividly before my mind; moved by the depth of the milk of Dharma, I cannot forget him even in old age. The circumstances of the master’s beginning and entry into the Way I often heard from his own lips; only his final move I do not know where it came to rest. In the dingdi year I traveled east and, attending the feast of the layman Shen Dingfan, paid homage at the master’s stupa at Qizhen; I then raised funds to build a stupa pavilion and set aside supporting fields, thus doing a little to fulfill a single thought. Seeing that Mr. Liaofan’s inscription was incomplete, I have summarized what I saw and heard of his conduct and made this biography to show to those who come. The master was the patriarch who restored the Chan way; alas, his pivotal sayings were not recorded, so there is no way to spread abroad his secret wonder.

Shi Deqing says: The single transmission of Bodhidharma passed down through the five houses, and after Jingshan of our Ming dynasty the lion’s string was about to fall silent. It was our master alone who, through Chan Master Fazhou, continued the threadlike pulse. Though he did not raise a great Dharma banner, yet when the great Dharma lay in primitive obscurity he stood forth and strove to revive its way, making people know that there is a matter beyond. In his depth of insight, the plain solidity of his conduct, and his never forgetting the rules in movement or rest, he still preserved the model of Baizhang. Surveying all quarters, even had there been men of attainment, none could have surpassed him. Was he not a teacher of gods and men for a whole age? I, Qing, am ashamed of my dull and inferior faculties, unable to carry on the family name, and I have failed the clear teaching. Yet as for the mind that bears the Dharma, I have not dared forget it for a single breath. Reverently I have set out the master’s life in outline, so that those who look on it later may have some way of seeing the men of old.
Biography of Chan Master Miaofeng Deng of the Imperially Founded Great Protector of the Nation Shengguang Monastery on Mount Wutai

The master’s Dharma name was Fudeng, his style Miaofeng; he was a man of Pingyang in Shanxi, of the Xu family, a descendant of Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period. When the master was just seven his parents met a year of famine and died without means for burial, only a mat to cover them. Bereft of both parents, at twelve he entered a nearby monastery to leave home, but was not well treated; at eighteen he fled, carrying a single gourd, to the eastern hills of Puban, where the monk Lang of Wangu Monastery at the Wenchang Pavilion lived. The master begged in the market by day and slept in the pavilion by night, and Lang took pity on him. Not long after, the Prince of Shanyin came traveling and, seeing the master, thought him remarkable, saying to Lang, “You should treat this boy well; one day he will surely become a great vessel.” Lang therefore kept him as a disciple. After a while there was a great earthquake at night; the people’s houses all collapsed and the master was buried. Lang searched for him in desperate haste, but he was unharmed. The prince then said to the master, “You have come through a great calamity without dying; this is no ordinary thing. Why do you not take the great matter of birth and death to heart?” The master was then twenty-two and at once vowed to travel far. The prince said it was not yet time: he should first go to Qiyan Monastery in the Zhongtiao Mountains, repair a hermitage, and shut himself in retreat there. The master asked instruction of a nearby Dharma master, who showed him the contemplation of the dharma realm, and in retreat he practiced Chan contemplation, standing like an arrow on the mark day and night for three years, until his mind opened in awakening. He then composed a verse and presented it to the prince, who read it and said, “This boy’s insight is already like this. If he is not broken of it he will surely go mad one day.” So he took a worn shoe, cut off the sole and sealed it up to send to him, writing a verse: “This stinking scrap of shoe-sole, sealed and sent to you — not for any other business, but to beat that poetry-making mouth of yours.” The master saw it, bowed to the Buddha, and hung it about his neck with a thread; from then on he said not a word. Three years later he broke out of retreat to see the prince, and now had the bearing of a great man. The prince was delighted and said, “Though you know the matter of your own portion, you have not yet heard the Buddhadharma and may fall into wrong views. In the Zhongjie Mountains there is a lecturer on the Śūraṅgama Sutra; go quickly and listen, and receive the full precepts.” The master was then twenty-seven. The prince said to him, “You are a monk who has never left the monastery gate — a frog in a well. There are many teachers in the south; you should go and consult them. When you return one day you can serve as this old man’s pilgrim staff.” He then himself prepared the master’s traveling gear, took off his own woolen coat and socks, wrapped them in rags, and handed them to him, saying, “This is against the cold.” The master accepted the teaching and at once, with a single gourd and one staff, went south to inquire, consulting teachers everywhere. He reached the Southern Sea and paid homage at Putuo, then returned to Ningbo, where he caught a seasonal illness and nearly died. Lodging at an inn, he could not obtain a drop of water; feeling about, he scooped water from a bath basin and drank it, and it was very sweet. At dawn he looked and saw it was exceedingly foul, and vomited violently. Suddenly he realized: “It tasted sweet and looked foul — purity and filth are only in the mind.” At once he broke into a great sweat and the illness was cured, though his whole body was covered with sores and swellings. He came to the southern capital in the winter of the first year of Longqing. It happened that my late master was lecturing on the Lotus Sutra at Tianjie, and I was his assistant lecturer, while the master took the duty of latrine cleaner. I rose early each day and, seeing the latrine clean, knew the attendant must be no ordinary man. Watching by night, I saw him carrying a lamp, sweeping and washing the sticks; drawing close, I found only a jaundiced-looking mendicant. I thought it strange. After a time the master fell ill and lay in the guest quarters; I went to visit him and found his body covered with sores, his hands unable to lift. I asked after his health. He said, “Karmic obstruction. Bodily illness is hard enough to bear; the illness of craving is harder to cure.” I asked what he meant. He said, “Whenever I see the steamed buns handed out at the communal meal, I hate that I cannot lay them all down.” I knew in my heart that he was a man of the Way. The next day I brought cakes and fruit in my sleeve and offered them to him; he swallowed them gladly and with great relief. I laughed and said, “This is a true man of the Way.” As we sat talking, he said, “Whenever I hear the master lecture, my mind opens and my understanding is released. How is one so young so wonderfully awake?” I said, “This is not the matter of one’s own portion. I intend to follow a teacher and travel far, to inquire into the one matter beyond.” Within ten days I could not find him; I knew he had slipped away, fearing to be a burden to me. When the master returned, the prince was overjoyed and asked what Dharma-personages he had seen. The master described the worthies and teachers he had met, and among beginners counted me as one man. From this the prince too remembered me. After his return the master had no mind for the world; he cut thatch in the deepest part of the Zhongtiao Mountains and dwelt alone with his shadow, abstaining from grain and drinking only water for three years, in which he awakened greatly. He sealed his mind with the Mirror of the School and entered deeply into the purport that all is mind. The prince daily honored the Three Jewels and, having completed a monastery in the southern hills, invited the master to live there; he also wished to seek the Northern Canon from the palace and urged the master to go himself. The master had lived long in the mountains and his hair had grown uncut; he therefore went to the capital with attendant officials. I was then begging in Chang’an, and the master, on horseback, happened to recognize me in the marketplace of Yan. When his lodging was settled he sought me out in the Western Hills. At first sight he said, “Do you know me?” I looked at him closely, saw his two pupils bright and clear, and suddenly recalled the sick mendicant of Tianjie. I said, “I know you.” The master said, “A changed head and altered face.” I said, “The original face is at ease as it is.” He laughed and bowed, and after the meal we parted. The next day I went to call on him and we talked through the night, bed to bed; he told me fully of the matter of seeking the canon. I said, “Since parting from you I have not gone a day without thinking of you. Now I have come seeking you especially; I have just come to see the capital, to settle a long-cherished fancy.” The master said, “If you do not cast me off, I shall go before you to drive off the dogs.” Then we parted. It was the winter of the renshen year of Longqing. In the third month of the following spring I traveled to Mount Wutai, intending to live there; but unable to bear the ice and snow, I returned to the capital gate to beg. Lord Wang Boyu, the Left Vice Minister of War, said to me, “The Dharma gate is desolate, and it is truly sad. Judging by your spirit, one day you will be a teacher of gods and men. Do not roam idly. As I look at the present, there is none fit to be your teacher; apart from Master Miaofeng there is no friend for you.” I said, “We have a long-standing pledge.” He said, “If you indeed go together, I shall be your ferryman.” That autumn the master finished making the canon and had packed for the journey. I arrived just then; he at once had me mount the cart, and without a word we set out together. When we reached Pu the prince was overjoyed; when the canon was installed we stayed for the winter retreat. It was the guiyou year, the first of Wanli. The master had long been uneasy that his two parents’ spirits were not properly settled and wished to rebury them in the hills; the prince’s local administrator Lord Zha and the prefect of Pingyang, Lord Hu Shun’an, each helped with the burial. In the first month of spring of the following jiaxu year I joined the master in retreat at Mount Wutai. Going east I took the road past my home village and buried my two parents together; I chose a high open site east of the city and buried them there and wrote the grave inscription. When this was done we came to Mount Wutai and settled at the Dragon Gate on the North Terrace, where in a heap of ice and snow we found a few old rooms and sheltered together. Three years passed. I constantly thought that I had no way to repay my two parents, and so I made a vow to write out the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood mixed with gold, pricking my own blood; the master likewise pricked his tongue and wrote out a copy in red. As the sutras neared completion the master wished to hold an assembly without restriction, and so went down the mountain to collect the means. Within a year the conditions were all gathered and he wished to expound the great Avatamsaka, setting the opening for the winter of the xinsi year, the ninth of Wanli. Earlier the holy mother, to benefit the late emperor and protect the imperial person, had repaired the Relic Stupa at Tayuan Monastery on Mount Wutai; as the work neared completion she sought an heir and sent officials to Mount Wutai. The assembly was then gathering at the new monastery. The master and I discussed it: “All that we disciples do is nothing but repaying our country’s root. We should dedicate everything to that — truly the loyalty of a single thought of a subject beyond the world.” The master agreed, and so the assembly opened in the eleventh month of that winter and was completed in the third month of spring of the following renwu year, lasting a hundred and twenty days. From the nine frontiers and eight provinces, monks and laymen came without a break in the road; at each meal there were never fewer than several thousand. When the assembly ended we sealed the remaining gold and grain and handed it to the community, and the master and I parted lightly with a single bowl. I went east to the sea lands, and the master went to Luya to build a hermitage and live there. Within a year the holy mother, on the matter of seeking an heir, inquired after the two of us and found the master alone; on the Luya she granted the building of Huayan Monastery, and presently it became a great teaching ground, with a ten-thousand-Buddha iron pagoda of seven stories built on the summit. Formerly Wangu Monastery at Puban was the master’s old mountain; it had a Tang-dynasty holy monk’s relic stupa of thirteen stories, three hundred feet high, and a great Buddha hall, all fallen into ruin. Lord Wang Jianchuan, the local Minister of War, proposed rebuilding, and invited the master to live there three years; the stupa and hall were made new. Soon after Lord Li Kuo’an, Grand Censor of Sanyuan, asked him to build a bridge over the Wei River; the master went for two years and when the work was done returned to Luya. Passing through Ninghua he saw a cliff of a thousand fathoms, flat as a palm, and delighted in it; he hewed out a cave thirty-five feet in depth, breadth and height, carved the worlds of the ten directions of the Avatamsaka, and depicted ten thousand Buddhas and bodhisattvas, precise and exquisite, so that it became a great teaching ground. Not long after, the Western Court of Xuanfu proposed building a great river bridge; the master answered the call and, measuring it, found the water broad and the sand deep, and built a bridge of twenty-three arches, which was also completed. The master had long vowed to cast three gilded images of the great beings and build three bronze halls to send to the three great mountains. In the spring of the jihai year he went with his staff to Lu’an to call on the Prince of Shen. The prince had just had a gilded Samantabhadra cast to send to Emei; the master spoke of the bronze hall matter, and the prince asked the cost. The master said each hall would need ten thousand in gold. The prince gladly undertook the one for Emei, prepared baggage and escort, and sent the master to Jingzhou to supervise the casting himself, drawing the cost from the prince. The hall was over ten feet in height and breadth, gilded and carved with Buddhas and bodhisattvas, exquisite beyond compare and unmatched in the world. When finished it was sent to Emei. Lord Wang Jiyu, Grand Censor and governor of Shu, heard the master had come and asked to see him; questioning him on the essentials of mind, he found agreement, and at once offered to help with the one for the Southern Sea. Copper was then bought in Shu and craftsmen engaged at Jingmen; when the work was done it was carried to Longjiang, but the monks of Putuo firmly refused it and it did not reach there. So a site was chosen at Mount Hua near the southern capital and the holy mother was petitioned to grant the building of halls, where it was installed, and it became a great monastery. The master then made the one for Mount Wutai, all the cost drawn from the people, and it too was soon completed. In the spring of the yisi year the master escorted it in person to Mount Wutai and proposed installing it at Xiantong Monastery in Taihuai; the emperor was informed and sent the eunuch Wang Zhong of the Imperial Horse Service, while the holy mother sent the attendant eunuch Chen Ru, each bringing treasury gold to inspect the site. A site was divined at the monastery and a hall built to enshrine it, work beginning in the fifth month of summer of the bingwu year. It was newly founded and built up, with brickwork for the seven places and nine assemblies, a great hall of six levels front and back, and encircling towers and pavilions rising in layer upon layer, magnificent in scale. The name granted was the Imperially Founded Great Protector of the Nation Yongming Monastery. When the work was finished he established the Avatamsaka assembly of the seven places and nine assemblies, with twelve hundred people great and small, inviting ten Dharma masters to expound the Avatamsaka Sutra, all costs from the privy purse. The splendor of that assembly had no precedent. When the master first entered Mount Wutai, finding the roads rugged, he had bridges built over the streams and a great road paved with stone for over three hundred li; he repaired the bridge at Fuping County, granted the name Puji, and built a reception hall as a resting place for travelers. Outside the Longquan Pass at Rencao Stone he built a tea hermitage, granted the name Huiji Cloister, giving out medicine and tea, with a fixed sum granted each year; he was then also granted the Dragon Canon and built a brick pavilion to enshrine it, afterwards founding the Hall of the Seven Tathāgatas. At Fuping he established the Long Life Estate in honor of the holy mother, building halls and pavilions seven levels deep, casting a welcoming Amitābha image thirty-six feet high, with mountain gate, bell and drum towers, and lodgings in two corridors, broad and spacious in scale, so that it became another great teaching ground, granted the name Ciyou Yuanming Monastery, with several hundred acres of supporting fields. While the master lived at Mount Wutai, in the midst of these works he also answered other calls. The governor of Shanxi asked him to repair the great bridge over the Hutuo River on the road at Guo County; the Prince of Jin asked him to repair the Great Pagoda Monastery in the provincial capital, and when the halls were done he also built a bridge in the provincial city ten li long, though the work was unfinished. In the ninth month of autumn of the renzi year the master returned to the mountain ill and put in order the teaching grounds he had built, establishing them above and below as communities of the ten directions, each with the right man, and sending all his former retinue back to their old mountains, keeping not one. On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, at the hour of mao, he passed away sitting upright. The master was born in the gengzi year of Jiajing and entered cessation in the renzi year of Wanli; he lived seventy-three years and had over forty Dharma rains. After his cremation the emperor heard of it and granted burial, and a stupa was built west of Yongming. Whatever of the master’s merit was unfinished, all was ordered completed; the holy mother granted a thousand in gold and five hundred bolts of cloth for the funeral. Earlier Censor Su Yunpu, touring Shanxi, had entered the mountain to visit the master and, finding agreement on the essentials of mind, exchanged verses and replies, most of which were not recorded. When the master showed illness he sent a doctor with medicine, and after his passing he composed the stupa inscription. He often said, “People take Master Miaofeng for a teacher of merit-fields, but truly do not know his transcendent awakening.” Alas, what a man the master was! Rising from lonely obscurity, he yet in the end performed the great Buddha-work of a whole age among gods and men. In my early years I discerned him amid lowly servitude; at thirty I traveled with him, vowing to practice. Then after one parting at Mount Wutai, more than thirty years passed, and at last, with a minor prince aiding the Way and finally the emperor, the holy mother and the princes as patrons, whatever he built, his Dharma gifts surged like clouds at a thought, and wherever he set his foot it became a jeweled monastery. By what condition could this be? Had his mind not roamed the dharma realm and this flowed from the inconceivable power of the ocean of the nature’s perfect fusion, could it have been so? From the time the master set out with his staff and lived in the mountains, he never had anything beyond one robe, and never one attendant with him. All that he built he undertook with a clear single mind, and gold and offerings never touched his fingers; whatever he established he at once left, with no care at all. Of the more than ten great monasteries he completed, not one had a disciple as resident keeper. Dwelling, he followed conditions; he was not the least bit self-seeking. Leaving, he seemed to forget it, not a thread clinging. He drifted like floating clouds gathering and scattering, like a lone crane coming and going. Was he not one who deeply realized mind-only and, meeting conditions, made them his school? The master’s features were ancient and his bones firm; he bore five uglinesses. His face was stern and cold, his feeling and consciousness cut off; he was solitary and strong, without any ornament. To the end of his life his ribs never touched a mat. I deeply felt the strength of his whetting and polishing; though we were friends in the Dharma, in truth I took him as my mind’s teacher. Though we parted for over thirty years, he was ever present before my eyes, as if I stood before a tutor. All my life I have not forgotten whence I came — was this not a karmic bond from former lives? Sadly I am old and cannot offer a stick of incense in his shrine. Because conditions obstruct the Way and the world is full of fleshly eyes that take the master for a merit-field and do not know his secret attainment, I have set out the master’s life in outline, so that later ages may know that in the more than two hundred years of our Ming, the work of establishing the Dharma gate belongs to this one man alone. How rarely is such a one seen!

The appraisal says: When the men of old once gained the true diamond eye, they could gather the long river into cream, turn the great earth into gold — no extraordinary feat. Yet within the emptiness of the Dharma nature these are but wild horses and dust motes, and so the master regarded himself. I have often secretly thought that if one could take conditions like the master’s and gather them into a single horizon as aids to the Way, building monasteries like Nālandā, planting both the nature and the characteristics schools and cultivating both Chan and Pure Land, then in forty years, without his shadow leaving the mountain, his merit for the Dharma gate would equal that of Qingliang and Donglin. The Avatamsaka Pure Land adorned before his eyes would be more than three mountains and ten monasteries. Alas, he is gone; perhaps we must await the master’s return.
Biography of Dharma Master Xuelang En, Restorer of the Dharma Way

Since the white horse came from the west and the teaching of images rose in the east, Kumārajīva and Vimalakīrti shook its main cords and Master Yuan drew out the threads of the Nirvāṇa, and the great Dharma first shone bright in the middle lands; the Six Dynasties were its flourishing. Yet its true lineage had not yet been greatly established. From the time Tiantai set forth the three contemplations and made a house of its own, and in the Tang Xianshou first opened the Avatamsaka dharma-realm school, Qingliang alone excelled in its beauty, while Xuanzang expounded the purport of consciousness-only and Kuiji devoted himself wholly to that gate — from this the sources of the nature and characteristics schools and the purport of one mind and three truths first spread across the earth. The holy teaching of our Buddha for a whole age was like the great sea flowing hidden beneath the four continents; its hidden doctrines were like the sun and moon lifted into mid-heaven. Thereafter writings multiplied at many gates and formulations were not one, but all plumbed the source and gathered back to the true, all swam in the Tathāgata’s ocean of nature and scooped up the fish and dragons of the dharma realm — no different from seeing the white curl between the brows at Vulture Peak or hearing the perfect voice in the garden of awakening. When Bodhidharma came from the west and established the purport of a single transmission, pointing directly at the one mind and not esteeming letters, then the teachings became the Buddha’s eye and Chan the Buddha’s mind, and Chan and the teachings drove abreast without conflict. But from the Sixth Patriarch onward, as the Chan way greatly flourished, there was no lack of rebuke for attachment, and teachings and Chan began to split. Guifeng tried in vain to pull them back; Yongming gathered nature and characteristics into the one mind and called it the Mirror of the School, and the Buddha-patriarchs’ whole substance and great function were made brilliantly clear. Then our Sage Ancestor rose like a dragon, cleared the world and opened an age of peace for ten thousand generations. On first reaching Jiankang, before sword and armor were put off, he honored the Buddhist teaching: in the third year of Hongwu he summoned the eminent monks of the realm and settled them at Tianjie Monastery, and established the assembly of universal deliverance at Linggu in the Zhong Mountains. The famous all gathered; the mysterious school was greatly expounded, and the imperial carriage came in person to hear the joy of Dharma, so that the flourishing of the Dharma way was no less than in former times. How magnificent! Within the one gate he established three teachings: Chan, lecture and Yogācāra — Chan to awaken to one’s own mind, lecture to clarify the Dharma nature, Yogācāra to rescue the dark realms. Three great monasteries were built: Tianjie to house the Chan monks, Tianxi for doctrinal study, and Nengren for Yogācāra — vast and overflowing, the whole realm paid court to them. After the move north, however, the Chan way was not made manifest; only the lecture school gathered in the great capital, and the Dharma way of Jiangnan daily faded into silence. In the Zhengde and Jiajing periods the lecture seats of the north were held only by the two elders Tong and Tai, sitting on the flower seat in the capital while scholars from within the seas gathered; southern scholars, accustomed to softness and warmth, looked up to them as to heaven. It was our late master the monk Wuji who, from Huaiyin, followed his teacher and went to rely on them with a single bowl; drinking ice and gnawing snow, forgetting sleep and food for over twenty years, he fully obtained the essentials of the nature and characteristics of Xianshou and Ci’en. Afterwards he returned south. When he came to Jinling the son of the Prince of Wei in the state of Wei saw him and was delighted, and became his patron, asking him to lecture on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra. He sang but none answered; his listeners were few. Lord Lu Wutai, a secretary of the Ministry of Rites, went to call on him and said to my late grand-master the monk Xilin, “I have lately met the eminent monk Wuji who has come from the north; he is truly a teacher of gods and men. Hearing his exposition of the wondrous meaning, I found it deeply in accord with the Buddha’s mind. I reflect that Bao’en was the lecture teaching established by the Sage Ancestor; how can the monks dwelling here be utterly without hearing of it? As abbot, if you could with courtesy invite him back to the monastery and greatly expound the Dharma way to open and guide the deluded, it would be a blessing for the Dharma gate.” My grand-master assented, and at once sent gifts with full courtesy and pressed the invitation. It was the thirty-second year of Jiajing. The master came and settled in the Tripiṭaka Hall of the monastery, where the relic stupa of Master Xuanzang stood. The community set out regular offerings each year, and my grand-master chose several dozen monks of the monastery and led them himself beneath the seat, hearing lectures on the sutras daily. A few elders of the neighboring mountains responded at first; in time the good men of the capital gathered daily, knowing to provide the four requisites, and the wind of wholesome transformation gradually opened. There was then a layman, Lord Huang, whose wife and he had long kept vegetarian; one day he took his young son Liulang to present offerings. Liulang was Dharma Master Xuelang En. By nature he was lofty and unrestrained, bright and unmatched among his fellows, fond only of play, which he made into Buddha-work. When he entered the village school the teacher instructed him in reading, but he gave it scarcely a thought; when pressed he only looked at him and grinned, quite unfit. On the day of the offering it happened that the Eight Consciousnesses Rule was being lectured; as soon as the boy heard it, it struck home in his mind, and he listened attentively and stayed two or three days. His father called him to go home and he would not answer. His father said, “Do you love to leave home?” The boy smiled and nodded. His father pressed him, but he would not return. When the father had been home some days the mother missed him sorely and urged the father to fetch him; the father came and pressed him again and again. The boy had secretly put scissors in his sleeve and slipped to the Tripiṭaka Stupa, where he cut off his own hair, and holding it up to his father said, “Take this back to mother.” The father wept bitterly; the boy only looked at him. So in the end he did not return. The father went back and told the mother, and they let him be. The boy was then twelve. From then on he was a novice, moving among the assembly with the bearing of a great man. One day at the communal meal he came first to the refectory and sat in the first seat. Presently the chief seat arrived and snapped, “How does a novice dare sit here?” He said, “Who should sit here?” The chief seat said, “One who understands the Buddhadharma.” He said, “Then I should sit here.” The chief seat said, “What Buddhadharma do you understand?” He said, “Please ask.” The chief seat said, “Then tell me what was lectured from the Dharma seat today.” The boy answered offhand, wholly to the point. The assembly marveled, saying, “This boy is a returned man.” Whenever he heard lectures he would play, yet when questioned nothing was missing. The year after he left home I was twelve and also left home; my grand-master took me to call on the late master. The boy was playing in the Buddha hall and, seeing me, his face lit with joy as if long intimate; people took us for brothers. Being young, I was occupied with recitation and did not know the meaning. In his youth he dwelt in lecture halls, and his insight surpassed the crowd, so that all respected and submitted to him. At eighteen he was already given a seat as assistant lecturer, and those who heard him were startled into understanding. Yet his nature was untrammeled and he gave it little thought. At nineteen I was shaved; the late master expounded the profound discourse on the Avatamsaka at our monastery, and I received the precepts and listened, my mind opening as if from former habit. Then he valued me and we became sworn brothers in the Dharma. He had not yet studied worldly letters; I happened to compose a poem on dwelling in the mountains, and he pasted it on the wall. His nephew, the scholar Huang, saw it and said enviously, “Uncle, you are much shamed by this man.” He said, “That is the craft of carving insects — hardly worth mentioning.” At twenty-one, steeped in the Buddhadharma, he roused himself and began to study worldly books, the philosophers, histories and the hundred schools, and ancient rhapsodies, poems and songs, searching them all, playing with the brush so that the meaning came before the stroke. The famous men of the three Wu he polished against until he had met nearly all; his poems were on every tongue, and a single note or word of his was treasured. He once said to me, “People say that without reading ten thousand scrolls one does not know Du Fu’s poetry; I say that without reading ten thousand scrolls one does not know the Buddhadharma.” He often read the great Avatamsaka commentary, and at the passage where bodhisattvas of the fifth ground must be broadly versed in the worldly learning of all schools before they can enter the world to benefit beings — his exertions there surely had a purpose. I was practicing Chan with my late master Yungu at Tianjie, my mind set on inquiring into the matter beyond. Whenever he saw me sitting withered, he would rebuke me: “What use are you, like a village shrine god?” He constantly prodded me to listen to lectures. I said, “Each follows his own aspiration. The ancients said that if one has penetrated the school of the self-nature, then looking back at letters is like pushing a door and having it fall into its socket — no difficulty at all.” He said, “If you truly can, I will treat you as my elder brother.” From then on my resolve for the mountain forests grew keener. Because I had first read the Avatamsaka I knew there was a Mount Wutai, and my heart flew there daily. At twenty-five I resolved to travel north and took leave of him at Xuelang Hermitage. He said, “Your constitution is weak, and the north is bitterly cold; you will hardly bear it. If you must, let me first take you roaming through the three Wu to temper your sinews, and then go — it will not be too late.” I said, “The three Wu are a pillow and mat to me. I know my lifelong habit of softness and warmth; unless I go where there is nothing to lean on, I will never cure it. This is my resolve.” He said, “If you must go, wait while I scrape together a little for the journey against wind and rain.” I laughed and said, “Brother, how long do you reckon my life to be?” He said, “How can one reckon such a thing?” I said, “Even if you could provision me for a year or a month, how could you provide for all my days?” He clung to the thought without end. I deceived him, saying, “If you cannot let it go, try to make some plan.” He went into the city through heavy snow, and I at once took my single gourd and went off for good. When he returned to the mountain and did not find me he burst into loud weeping. From this his whole life is known. So I went north alone with my staff; he too traveled to Songshan and returned after spending the winter at Funiu. He used to say, “Brother Qing has gone; I have no friend now.” Hearing that I was in the capital, he came seeking with gourd and hat, but I was on pilgrimage elsewhere, and so he stayed in the capital. When I and Master Miaofeng entered Mount Wutai and dwelt in a thatched hut, he heard of it and at once climbed the mountain, seeking me in the heaps of ice and snow. Talking at night, I pressed him on his resolve. He said, “I see that my mind is like ice; I vow to die and live together with you. Only I think of our old master, who is aged — what is to be done?” I said, “Not so. Each man has his own aspiration and his own conditions. As I see your conditions, they lie in spreading the Dharma to continue the wisdom-life, not in dry solitude. The Dharma way of Jiangnan has long been buried; happily our master the monk, entrusted by the Buddha, has opened it. Looking at his seat, it seems there is none to raise the family’s voice. You are the true son who can carry the house. The burden of the Dharma way in future is no light one, and the master is in his late years; without you, how shall he glorify the past and open the future? Go back quickly and do not linger long in other parts.” He at once prepared his staff to return. As he was about to set out I charged him: “You have never taken the Dharma on yourself. This time, while the master is old, take your place at his seat and gather the hearts of scholars from the four quarters; when one day you ascend the platform, it will be our family’s own possession. Do not decline too much.” After he returned he stood forth and took the Dharma as his charge, and the long-time students all fell back. Since the late master began spreading the Dharma he had three times expounded the great commentary and seven times lectured on the profound discourse, and the master fully obtained the purport of the Avatamsaka dharma realm, perfect and unobstructed; swimming in the ocean of the nature, he was called unmatched in his time. He had always admired the Chan school, and when Great Master Dazhang opened the hall at Shaolin he packed his bundle and went to consult, though it came to nothing.
