Afterwards Master Ang Xun’an came from Shaoshi to Qixia and raised kōans; the master humbled himself and followed him, discussing the ancient worthies’ pivotal occasions, and obtained the purport of the single transmission. Some were ashamed for him; he said, “Mañjuśrī was the teacher of seven Buddhas — what harm in striking the block for Śākyamuni?” From then on all his speech was free of constraint. He settled his mind in Chan contemplation. When the late master passed away the master took the flower seat, and daily ten thousand fingers encircled him. One day he turned completely about, swept away all the vulgar habits of commentary and exegesis, and raised only the root text, probing directly into the Buddha’s meaning, holding up the purport beyond words. He always taught students to enter by way of principle-contemplation, and so the eyes and ears of students were made utterly new, like gazing into the long sky, brushing aside clouds and mist to see sun and sky. The Dharma thunder woke the hibernating; all creatures revived, and none who heard but sighed that they had never known such a thing. Previously the lecture halls had mostly been plain and unlettered, and the doctrines they entered were like hugging a post while rowing — scarcely any capacity for transcendence. When the master appeared it was like a maṇi jewel shining all around, its five colors fresh, answering each in its own direction, one rain soaking all, the three grasses and two trees all receiving moisture. He embraced with compassion and broke with severity; for a time all the clever and outstanding men came out from beneath his seat. He taught the Dharma from first to last for nearly thirty years. At each period the assembly often numbered ten thousand fingers. Even wandering among mountains and waters, wherever his staff went, following conditions as he pleased, by waterside or under trees, he would wave his whisk according to his nature, like a dragon rearing or a tiger roaring, wind rising and clouds following. Never since ancient times had the north and south seen such a flourishing Dharma seat. The late master taught the Dharma for over thirty years, and of his disciples only two or three appeared in the world, nor did they greatly flourish. The master’s disciples who can be counted mostly spread and transformed in the four quarters; the masters of the Dharma seats north and south all came from his gate. Apart from Yexi San and Mingming Zong, already gone, there are now Chaosong Qin and Yiyu Run, who greatly sing forth in the three Wu; Yunpu Yu, who late revived the capital; Ruomei Zhi, who alone raised the banner in Jiangxi; and Xinguang Min, who proclaims in the north of the Huai. Wherever in the realm one is called a Dharma lecturer, all trace back to the master’s gate. Without the power of the four means of gathering, how could this be? Alas, how could it be measured by ordinary standards? Whenever the master left the seat he practiced wall-gazing. Once in the Changxing Mountains he built a hut for quiet practice and entered samādhi for two days, so that the trees and buildings shook; this no one knew. By nature he was broad and easy, without guile, not avoiding censure, taking fitness as his joy, coming and going freely like a lone crane in the sky, free of all constraint. Chan Master Daguan was somewhat resentful of him. I said, “You do not know Xuelang. I observe his causal ground: he aroused the mind hearing Consciousness-Only and cut his hair at the Relic Stupa — he is a returned man, the later body of Kuiji.” Master Da nodded and said, “From today I shall not dare look lightly on this man.” In the last years of Jiajing, lightning fire struck our monastery, and halls and shrines were ashes in a night. The master and I wept together and said, “Alas, the Buddha said that when the great fire burns the Pure Land is not destroyed; how could it be consumed with the rest? How sad and hard! In these times, if not we two, who else? Pity that we are young, of little merit, without the power of the Way. From now on we resolve to practice; when we have grown in time and our horns are high, we shall at last fulfill this vow of restoration.” So I went north, my resolve fixed on the great matter of birth and death, yet in my heart for over twenty years I never forgot it a single day. At Mount Wutai and the Eastern Sea we were like Zhang Liang to the end loyal to Han. Then unhappily I brought calamity on myself; truly the great causal matter cannot be sought by deluded thought. When I met with disaster and was exiled, passing my home village, the master took leave of me by the river and we talked knee to knee through the night of our first resolve. I said, “The moment had come; had I not met this fall, it would have been done within days. Now what is to be done? I am going. Brother, watch the times and sing first; you should beg in person in the southern capital to alert people’s eyes and ears. If Heaven grants me life and return sooner or later, it may still be reckoned.” The master nodded. At dawn I went far away. It was the eleventh month of the winter of the yiwei year of Wanli. In the third year after I crossed the ranges, in the wuxu year, the master saw that the top of our monastery’s pagoda was leaning and resolved to repair it. The authorities of the time helped, and the supervising secretary Lord Zhu sang first; the master himself led several hundred men, begging in the markets in due order. For a time people’s hearts leaped up and money gathered in hundreds and thousands at a move, and the great work was undertaken. The pagoda was twenty-five fathoms high, and the core-pole for the top about seven fathoms long, with scaffolding half again as much; it had to come down from the sky like a mustard seed into a needle’s eye — a hard feat. The master’s heart labored to extremity and he suddenly vomited several pints of blood. Then the pole went in, and those on the scaffolding were like birds on a tender branch, yet not one was harmed. Was this not the work of mind-power? The total cost was tens of thousands of strings of cash; only three thousand in gold came from the holy mother, the rest from the people, without a hair from the public coffers. The master was born in a wealthy house, and all thought him soft by habit; yet in middle age his conduct was stricter than austerities. At Dajin in Jiangdong he established a free-tea hermitage and carried water himself, offering it daily without wearying; his disciples followed and he never ceased teaching. Even the weak grew daily stronger. He often thought of forming a rice-gruel bond with the ten directions, and in his late years went to Wangting in Wu and opened a reception hall, receiving travelers, himself fetching firewood and water and handling the implements, leading students in their work; by day they ate, in the evening they bathed, at night he taught the Dharma — both benefits given together. The scholars of the three Wu all believed and turned to him, and even the icchantikas became protectors of the Dharma. Not long after he showed a slight illness. One day he told the assembly, “Guard yourselves well; I am going.” His disciples begged him to leave a parting word. He said, “Like flowers in the sky, originally nonexistent — what is there to say?” They asked, “If you pass, shall we use a sitting shrine or a coffin?” He said, “Die sitting, use a shrine; die lying, use a coffin. Striking the tin and beating the bottle — do not make arrangements.” With that he presently asked for a bath and changed his clothes, and passed away sitting upright. His disciples received him for burial at Xuelang Mountain; on the day of cremation grief filled the roads, and students mourned as for a parent. The master was born on the ninth day of the ninth month of the yisi year of Jiajing and entered cessation on a certain day of a certain month of the dingwei year of Wanli, living sixty-three years with forty-five rains-retreats. Of the disciples he ordained, though many, only his grandson Huijing, styled Yuandu, fully obtained the essentials of mind and was skilled in the characteristics school; his treatise on Consciousness-Only was indeed opened and developed by him. Pity that he died young. Of his Dharma-transmitting disciples who appeared in the world, they are as listed above; those hidden and obscure are still many. Alas, the master and I were as brothers born of the same womb; parted for thirty years, we never joined again in old age, and I sigh over it from time to time. I think that in the present age those who know the master are few — how much more after his death? So I have set out his life in outline, for the restoration of the Dharma way hangs on it, and to let later students know that the causal conditions of the great Dharma have their source.

The appraisal says: I have heard that when bodhisattvas come and go among gods and men, leaving affliction to moisten their rebirth, they still have the dimness of a womb between lives and do not penetrate past lives; only they verify it in dreams, and the wise observe it through habit — not the least deviation. From the master’s circumstances in leaving home I know he must be a returned man. The perfected move secretly through the world, playing with it, backward or forward without fixed rule — how can ordinary feeling measure them? Elephants and dragons trample; it is no ground for a lame donkey. No wonder fleshly eyes slighted him. Had he not ridden the power of former vows, how could his light flow into the last age and raise up the decline of a hundred generations? From the ease of his birth and death it can be known.
Biography of Chan Master Langmu Zhi, Restorer and Abbot of the Great Avatamsaka Monastery on Mount Fu at Wancheng

The master’s Dharma name was Ben Zhi; he was first styled Huiguang, a son of the Li family of Qujing. His forebears were men of Jinling who later moved to southern Yunnan. From birth he was spirited and unmatched, bearing the will to leave the dust. South of Qu city is Mount Langmu, and the master’s father left home and dwelt there, styled the monk Baizhai. At twelve the master went to him to leave home and was shaved as a servant boy. Later, on pilgrimage, he met the secretary Huang Daoyue and, finding their talk in accord, had his style changed to Langmu. Baizhai took the Avatamsaka as his work, and the master, roused by what he heard, at once devoted himself to it, keeping the great matter of birth and death in his heart and fixing his will on the beyond. At nineteen he received the full precepts. As Baizhai was about to pass from the world the master asked his instruction; Zhai said, “How do you know he will not be a son-in-law before nightfall?” The master was stung, and at once resolved to travel. He went north through the central plains, visiting every famous mountain, consulting teachers, his footprints over half the realm and his spirit swallowing eight or nine parts of every quarter. The great elders of the Dharma gate north and south — Dafang and Yinzong of Funiu, Wujin of Nanyue, Da’an of Mount Lu, Bianrong and Yuexin of Jimen — were all masters of teaching and Chan in their day, and he entered all their gates and passed through their forge and hammer. Thus in both the school and the teachings he obtained the guiding purport; yet in the one matter of inquiring into his own portion he took non-awakening as his urgency. So he stood in meditation for twelve years and at last the light of mind shone through, and from then on his wit and eloquence were free. On pilgrimage north he passed through Lu’an, and Lord Liu, a grandee, established the Xinzhongfeng Avatamsaka hermitage for him. Before long he left for Baixia. The supervising secretary Zhong Yuchun was a man who scorned others and had always slighted the Dharma gate, and none dared cross his blade. One day he came to Tianjie Monastery and asked the one in charge, “In this Dharma gate of universal welfare, is there any Chan man?” The one in charge pushed the master forward to see him. Zhong asked, “Chan master, is Tianjie Monastery inside the mind or outside it?” The master said, “Set the monastery aside. May I ask what you take for your mind?” Zhong was silent. The master said, “Never mind Tianjie — the three thousand Buddhas are only on the tip of this mountain monk’s whisk.” After a long while Zhong bowed, and from then on knew that there were men in the Dharma gate. The official Tao Yunyi of the ministry was his sworn friend; when Tao was demoted to the assistant prefect of Luzhou and administered Lu’an, he founded Jingxin Retreat to await the master. Ninety li east of Wan is Mount Fu, where formerly Master Yuan and Lord Ouyang discoursed on the Dharma over a chessboard; there was an ancient Avatamsaka teaching ground, ruined and abandoned by an icchantika. The Hanlin scholar Lord Wu Guanwo often grieved over it and wished to restore it but could not. The master came drifting from the Fei River with a single staff, and Lord Wu, seeing him and speaking with him, found their minds sealed in agreement. He bowed twice and said, “Fudu was indeed the seat of the nine-belt school, and lately the place where the monk Gutting spread transformation; the Avatamsaka teaching ground is where the banner should be raised again. Now it is carried off by the powerful — what is to be done for this mountain? Gutting was a man of southern Yunnan; are you, master, his later body come at the right time? Is this not the fulfillment of a former vow?” The master heard and was astonished, saying, “In my youth I would gaze endlessly at Gutting’s flesh-body; and I had heard that he opened the Dharma at Fudu, not knowing it was this very mountain. Remembering that the Avatamsaka was the beginning of my leaving home, all seems a former bond.” So gladly he gave his assent in his heart. He burned incense and prayed to the Dharma-protecting gods, then slung his bundle and left. The Hanlin scholar still did not know where he was bound. When the master reached Huaiyin, Lord Liu Dongxing, Grand Censor of Qinshui, was stationed there and had long sought friends beyond the world; meeting by chance at Longxing Monastery and seeing the master’s ready wit, he was delighted and lodged him in his own residence. In leisure they talked, and the matter of Fudu came up. Lord Liu said gladly, “That is the work of a finger-snap.” He at once sent orders down to the prefecture and county, and in one move the icchantika was cowed and all our fields of Wenyang were returned. A ruin of a hundred and fifty years was raised up by a single word — was this not the power of a vow? When the monastery was restored the master went north into the capital. It happened that the emperor, for the holy mother the Empress Dowager, had issued and distributed the honored canon; the master received the sealed letter, carried the canon, and returned with it to Mount Fu. Beginning in the wuxu year and ending in the renyin, in the space of five years the Great Protector of the Nation Avatamsaka Monastery of Mount Fu rose towering as if from the earth. How could this be human effort? When the community was settled he entrusted it to his disciple Yuan, and, grateful to Lord Liu for protecting the Dharma, went to Qinshui to offer condolences. The Prince of Shen was an armor of the Dharma and foremost among kṣatriyas; hearing the master had entered his domain he wished to meet him. The master said to the envoy, “The Dharma is entrusted to kings, and I have long looked up to the worthy prince’s deep resolve to protect the Dharma from without. If we meet by worldly convention, I dare not disgrace the prince’s bright virtue.” The envoy reported this to the prince, who said he wished to hear the essentials of the Dharma. At dawn the prince sat in the central hall and invited the master in. Standing, the master bowed and asked the prince, “Excellent, lord of the world, rich in lands, noble beyond compare — by what surpassing cause did you obtain this wondrous fruit?” The prince said, “I cultivated it among the Three Jewels.” The master said, “If you cultivated it among the Three Jewels, why do you not bow when you see a monk, and give rise to great pride?” The prince was startled and came down from his seat, invited him into the Hall of Preserved Mind, burned incense, bowed, and asked the essentials of the Dharma. He then asked about the Avatamsaka’s chapter on pure conduct: “Body, speech and mind; Buddha, Dharma and Sangha — none of them is pure conduct; in the end what is pure conduct?” The master said, “In the place where all are not, there precisely is pure conduct.” The prince heard with joy and observed the courtesy of a disciple. Of all the offerings he accepted only one purple robe and a crystal rosary, which he left to guard the gate of Fudu. The prince also became a patron of the Avatamsaka. Though the master came and went in the capital, he never met the old man Zibai face to face. In the winter of the guimao year the old man met with royal persecution, and the confused were shaken and dazzled. The master sighed, “Zibai not only used contrary means to transcend birth and death, which is most rare, but with one death repaid the ruler’s forty years of honoring the teaching. Without this old man, would the Dharma gate not be wholly buried in a single bowl?” Those who know said the master had seen Zibai in person. The Hanlin scholar Wu said, “For one who knows the master, why must it be a disciple?” After the one change in the Dharma gate the monasteries of the capital were shaken and each man feared for himself; even those long famed as masters scattered like startled birds and fish. The master alone sat at ease on the diamond ground as the hall of the Māra host. Yet none knew his subtle intent — was this not speaking a turning phrase on Zibai’s behalf? Two years later, in the winter of the yisi year, when the holy mother had completed three hundred and sixty sixty-year cycles, an assembly was held at Guangci south of the capital to add to her longevity; by her decree the master was invited to expound the Śūraṅgama Sutra. He did not at first accept, but when pressed he began; before finishing the second fascicle, at the passage on the deluded views of identity and difference, he suddenly told the assembly, “Birth and death, coming and going, are all what the eye-disease sees. I am going. The adornment of the Avatamsaka is what I have depicted; now I return.” He sat upright on the seat and passed away. It was the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month of the yisi year of Wanli. Among his lay disciples who obtained his strength, only the Ink-Pool Layman Wang Shunding, a bureau director in the Ministry of War, was there: three days earlier the master had written to take leave of him, saying he would set out and hoped to meet once to settle this vastness, and entrusting him with his affairs. Wang’s reply asked, “At the time when the dripping water freezes, how is it before your eyes?” A day later he passed away. When the news reached the holy mother she grieved and granted gold. His relics were returned to the southern foot of Wondrous Peak on Fudu, according to his wish. The whole story is recorded in the Hanlin Wu’s stupa inscription. Living beyond the ranges, I heard the master’s name stir the age, and monks coming and going proclaimed that his character was tall and wonderful, with nothing in his breast and no one in his eyes. From youth he had walked on pilgrimage, charging through every quarter like a lion slipped from its rope — how could he be compared to those who trudge with bundle and bamboo hat? Seeing the swiftness of his wit, he must have been a seed of wisdom from former roots, borne here on the wheel of vow. Master Yuan opened Mount Fu, and after a hundred years it fell; in time Gutting raised it again. Gutting raised it for a hundred years, and the master restored it in his own day. From this we see: was Gutting not the later body of Master Yuan, and the master not the echo of Gutting? Looking at his conduct, he was like an illusory man. The Grand Historian said, “Gutting’s road home is the road he came by; Yuan’s record of the school entered by way of the teachings.” This is a true record. Though the master did not lead a multitude, in his last move his tongue-root remained unbroken.

The appraisal says: I have heard that the Buddhas do not abandon the realm of beings and bodhisattvas do not cut off the root of birth and death. Hence the solitary liberation of the one-sided is rebuked as scorched and spoiled; how could holding to extinction be true practice? Moreover, the teachers Sudhana consulted were all manifested from the light between Vairocana’s brows; therefore in the Avatamsaka dharma realm blades of grass and motes of dust are all bodhisattva practice. So we know that the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old, appearing and disappearing in the ocean of the three realms, see the taste of a hundred rivers in a single drop. Looking at the master from first to last, he took the Avatamsaka as ultimate and could transform birth and death as illusion: this is to reach the unborn by way of conditions having no nature, and the master truly had it.
Biography of the Novice Jingming

The novice was a Mr. Huang of Qiantang. Because at the point of death he asked to be shaved and departed sitting in a monk’s form, he is called a novice. His secular name was Cheng Hui, his style Yuanfu. He first took refuge with Master Yunqi and was given the Dharma name Jingming. By nature he was uncompromising all his life, out of step with the world, caring nothing for livelihood; in his village he offended many. Even at gatherings of kin and friends he would only sit slumped and staring. He was indifferent and without cravings; beyond mountains and waters, brush and ink, he had no affairs. When his father died he left no property, and he could barely feed eight mouths. He was deeply filial, serving his grandmother, his birth mother and his adoptive mother; even when in straits and unable to continue dainties, he did his utmost in every way. When his grandmother died, though gravely ill and bedridden, he exerted himself to the utmost in the funeral rites, and the village praised him. He loved to give: when an old neighbor woman had no clothes for the cold he took off his own coat and clothed her; when a poor neighbor had no food he emptied his purse of its last hundred coins and gave them all. His wife’s brother, a certain Wen, seeing that he was solitary and hard enough to enter the Way, spoke to him often; he was pleased but did not enter. So he was led to take refuge at Yunqi and received the name. In the winter of the renzi year he contracted a blood-spitting illness that did not heal for three years. In the spring of the yimao year, gravely ill and weary of his home, he moved to the Shao family garden east of the city. The Wen brothers drew him to recite the Buddha’s name, but his mind would not engage, for he had never set his will on this and was not yet willing to die. Wen, stirred, cried out in a stern voice, “After your eyesight falls to the ground, where does this that now knows pain and ache finally fall?” The young man started and changed color, saying, “What is to be done?” Wen then urged him strongly to recite the Buddha’s name. He asked, “Shall I recite the Amitābha of my own nature, or the Amitābha of the Pure Land?” Wen said, “Do you think there are two?” Ming suddenly had an insight. He asked Dharma Master Huiwen to come and set up an image for contemplation, and to explain the conditions of the Pure Land; as the Dharma sounds entered his ear he was glad. He urgently asked Wen to arrange for his shaving, received the novice precepts, and put on the Dharma robe. Looking at himself in a mirror, he said, “Now I have a place to die.” He then shut out his family and recited the Buddha’s name with all his strength, silently contemplating the lotus for seven days, and the whole household smelled the fragrance of lotuses. At the point of death he suddenly broke into a smile and murmured a verse: “I brought nothing here; I take nothing away. On the summit of the high mountain, one round of autumn — this is the original true meaning.” He then had his family prepare a vegetarian meal to offer to the Buddha and invited pure companions to recite the Buddha’s name, dedicating the merit with the vow-text, until the passage on the Buddha’s radiant light receiving and guiding, his hand stretched down to lift the dying. His joyful look was visible; he rose and sat upright, opened his eyes and gazed steadily at the Buddha image, and passed away in peace. It was a certain day of a certain month of a certain year.

The Illusory Man says: I have heard it said of prajñā that it is like a great fire: the swiftest insect can alight everywhere, but cannot alight on a fire. The minds of beings can reach everywhere, but cannot reach prajñā. So we know that one in the burning house whose nature is firm and uncompromising and who does not accord with worldly feeling is so by the power of prajñā perfuming him from within through former habit — only he is deluded and does not see it himself. Look at Mr. Huang, who never once thought of the Way, and when his illness grew grave, relying on the strength of kin and friends, was pointed back to the true path; at the brink of death he roused the mind to leave home, became a novice, put on the Dharma robe and went to his death. Reciting the Buddha’s name for seven days, he could at once move the Buddha to receive and guide him, and he passed away sitting upright. Is this not the proof of prajñā’s perfuming? As it is said, one thought of turning the light back is instantly the same as the original possession — the young man truly had it. Who says birth and death are hard to escape?
A Brief Biography of the Younger Master Wen

The younger master was of the Wen family, named Qichu, styled Ziyu, a man of Qiantang in Zhejiang and the younger brother of the provincial graduate Qixiang. As a child he was sickly and so early gave up the examinations, having long held the will to escape birth and death and no mind for a household. He took refuge with Yunqi and received the Pure Land gate, believing deeply and practicing with strength. When I went to mourn at Yunqi, the younger master bowed and said, “For the great matter of birth and death, I wish to be shaved and follow after the teachers.” I said, “Not so. The Buddha-nature cannot be confined by the four elements — how could hair obstruct it? Moreover, your parents are alive and you may not travel far; how could a son of the Buddha be unfilial?” So he let it be. When I returned to Mount Kuang I learned that he was gravely ill and near death, and I grieved for him. Then I read his elder brother’s account and was overjoyed, saying, “Truly a heroic man!” At first the younger master trusted in the strength of his own faith; though long ill, his mind was strong, and he was certain that rebirth would be easy. But when the end came, in the very midst of being born and dying, his accumulated habits appeared before him and his mind and spirit were confused; then he knew that his pure karma was not yet unmixed and that coming and going was not easy. So he leaped up and cried out, “Quick, get the teachers to recite the Buddha’s name to help me!” When the teachers had gathered and had recited for several days, yet the habitual realms still clouded and disturbed him, he cried out again, “The root-stock of birth and death — I know it cannot be pulled up by another!” He rose at once, put on his clothes, washed, burned incense before the Buddha and burned his arm, repenting with earnest and sorrowful sincerity through the whole night without wearying. Presently he knew for himself that his former obstructions had melted like ice, his mind was at peace and his spirit at ease, and the true realm of the Pure Land shone clear before him. Serene and still, he urgently had himself shaved, put on the robe and assumed the monk’s form, took leave of the assembly in peace, and passed away sitting upright. Alas, how could this be within the power of an ordinary man? I have often heard that nirvāṇa is the peaceful dwelling of all Buddhas, and that without incalculable aeons of hardship it cannot be realized; yet the butcher Wide Forehead laid down his cleaver and at once ascended to the Pure Land, the old home of beings. There are even those sunk in the cauldron of boiling water who, at one thought of turning the light back, are changed into a lotus pond of the eight virtues. Of these two I have heard the words but not seen the men. Looking at the younger master, when at the end the habitual realms appeared before him, was that not a foretaste of the evil paths? How heroic that he leaped up, and with one great shout of anger pulled out the root of beginningless birth and death and changed the bitter destination into a Pure Land — was he not a man of mettle? This Way, again, cannot be done with voice and smiling countenance. The younger master’s conduct is fully recorded in his elder brother’s account; I therefore single out the outline, so that those who discuss the gate of rebirth may find in him a good proof.

Inscribed After Chan Monk Ruizhi Lin Wrote Out the Avatamsaka Sutra in His Own Blood — Written in Prison

The Flower Store is the sutra that unites the whole dharma realm. It points directly to Vairocana’s ocean of fruition, where the virtue of the nature is perfect and unobstructed, vast and free, subtle and adorned, and shows it as the daily life of beings, the gate of the equal mind-ground realized here and now, so that through it the dust of habit may be swept away, the true realm revealed as inseparable from this very place, and measureless enjoyment obtained at once. Consider: Buddha is equal, beings are equal; lands and dust-motes, defiled and pure, are equal; kalpas and thought-moments, coming and going through the three times, are equal; delusion and awakening, cause and fruit, principle and phenomena, are equal. Such is the nature of things, and they abide so of themselves. That they appear unequal is solely because we are blind to a single mistaken thought, so that in the end there is a gulf between heaven and abyss: as it is said, when feeling arises wisdom is blocked; when thought changes the essence differs. Hence the saying: “How wonderful, how wonderful! All beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue-marks, but because of deluded, inverted attachment they do not realize them. If they leave deluded attachment, then natural, effortless wisdom appears at once — as a single dust-mote contains the scriptures of a great chiliocosm, and a wise man, seeing clearly, splits it open and brings them out, and its usefulness is inexhaustible.” Seen in this light, whether or not beings possess it in their minds depends only on whether the eye is clear at this moment — what else is there? Therefore Mañjuśrī raised it as wisdom, Samantabhadra wielded it as practice, Sudhana took it up to arouse the bodhi mind, and Maitreya carried it to the fruit. The forty-two stages each realize it; the fifty-three teachers wholly raise it. The moon fills the three contemplations; stars array the ten gates. Arrangement and perfect fusion, phenomena and principle without obstruction, down to the mutual entry of dust-motes and hairs, the mutual adornment of environment and being — all the various words and remoter dharma-images, the liberation in the fire-heap and knife-mountain, the firm endurance lying on thorns or serving as ox or dog, even the hidden passage of other kinds of beings and the scattering of divided bodies and shadows — none of it is anything but the sharp instrument that plays its blade within a dust-mote. With the instrument the dust-mote is easily broken; the dust-mote broken, the scriptures come forth; the scriptures come forth, the virtue of the nature is revealed; the virtue of the nature revealed, the ocean of fruition is complete; the ocean of fruition complete, nothing is lacking. Even so, six thousand attaining the Way beneath his words is still a dull faculty; to call Samantabhadra three times when he stands before your eyes — how is that a wisdom eye? Truly, deaf and blind, sealed up in consciousness and feeling, beings use it daily and do not know it. If they knew, then the senses, their objects, the consciousnesses and their realms, blades of grass and motes of dust, would all be the true sutra of the dharma realm; bending and stretching, looking up and down, coughing, spitting, swinging the arms, would all be Samantabhadra’s wondrous practice. With such a sutra, an ocean of ink could not finish copying it; with such a practice, daily life as it appears is more than enough. It lies only in the power of one thought of turning the light back to shine within. Now the Chan monk Lin has written this sutra in drops of his own blood. Did he write it after clear seeing, or did clear seeing come after the writing? Or did he write it wishing to see, without yet having seen? If he wrote after clear seeing, then without lifting the brush the whole sutra was already present, as before a precious mirror — why then the dripping ink, the petty labor over slips and characters? If clear seeing came after the writing, then in his present daily life the wondrous realm is fully manifest, like a net of hanging pearls — why then the darkened karmic consciousness, wandering vaguely in a world of water-moon and sky-flowers? If he wrote wishing to see without having yet seen, then to split bone for a brush, flay skin for paper, prick blood for ink, dab and dye the great void, splash and scatter gold dust — does this not pile delusion on delusion and waste labor? Yet when one leaf falls, autumn returns to the whole world; when the reed-ash flies, spring rises in the whole earth. Therefore whether he writes or not, the whole sutra abides of itself; whether he sees or not, bright and dim are one suchness. Alas, a boat hidden in a night ravine is carried off by a strong man and one does not notice; when one notices, one steps out through Vairocana and the whole dharma realm is revealed, shining clear between hair-tip and eyelash, and in every thing and every encounter one brushes arms with Samantabhadra. Master Xiu said, “Who else but you will roam with me in the ocean of the Avatamsaka nature?” Otherwise, close your door a while and try turning back, and consult the Great Being Mañjuśrī again. Go now, and do not forget what has been enjoined.
Inscribed After Copying the Avatamsaka and Lotus Sutras

Vairocana, having realized the dharma realm to its end, is rich with a treasury of measureless merit, which is possessed in common by all beings and which they ought to obtain. Therefore he looks on all beings as his only child, and must wholly bestow what he himself has obtained before he is content. Though beings are blind and unaware of it, he sets up measureless skilful means and every kind of taming, and will not rest until they believe with certainty and without doubt. It is like a rich elder who possesses measureless wealth and has but one son, who fled away when young. Though the son turned his back on his father, the father never forgot him for a single thought. After long years the son returned as a hired laborer and did not recognize his father; but the father, knowing his son, lowered himself and humbled his pride, worked alongside him and grew close to him, and gradually let him know the truth, until their hearts trusted one another and father and son forgot their feelings; then he himself charged him in writing and handed over the whole family estate before he died, and only then was without regret. From this we know that the Flower Store is the record-deed within our Tathāgata’s treasury of the dharma realm, and the Lotus Sutra is like the elder’s written charge handing over the family estate. Only by entering these two gates of Dharma is one a son able to carry the house. The good man Wu Dajing has copied out the two sutras by hand — is he not one who knows his original possession and sets the Tathāgata’s household affairs in order? From this he must one day obtain what he ought to obtain.
Colophon to the Diamond Prajñā Sutra Written in Blood

Prajñā gives birth to all Buddhas, and so is the mother of the Buddhas and the Buddha-nature of beings. Thus what flows from prajñā flows on without end, like the sea flowing hidden beneath the earth of the four continents. Buddhas and beings are, in their very substance, without duality; so we know that the four elements and the root of beings, flesh, bone and blood, are all outflowings of prajñā, and tracing them to their source they are one substance without two. The layman He Xueren has pricked his blood to write out the Diamond Prajñā, to repay his parents — like leading a slender stream back to the sea. He may be called one who is skilled at returning to the root and repaying the root. Can any in the world who speak of great filial piety surpass this?

In Sanskrit, prajñā; in Chinese, wisdom. This is the great root of all Buddhas and beings. Deluded, it becomes birth and death; awakened, it becomes nirvāṇa. The Buddhas realize it as fundamental wisdom; beings turn from it and it becomes the stream of ignorance. In substance it is one; only bright and dim differ. Therefore our World-Honored One appeared in the world precisely to reveal and point out this wisdom. Because the Dharma was great and the capacities small, they could not receive and bear it, and so only after twenty years did he speak this sutra. He had already revealed it in many ways, desiring that they believe this wisdom with certainty and without doubt and use it as the root of Buddhahood. And this sutra is named Diamond because this wisdom is the diamond mind realized by the Buddha. Since he would take the enlightenment of the fruition ground as our causal mind, he made prajñā the first gate of entering the Great Vehicle. So we know the sutra is named Diamond not as a borrowed metaphor. Alas, all beings are deluded as to this fundamental wisdom and wander in birth and death — it is long since this began. Readers only think the sutra’s meaning profound and its words repetitive, and so hard to enter; they do not know that it takes emptiness as its school, the sudden cutting off of the root of doubt, and the straightforward mind and right mindfulness as its root, and that originally there are no words to establish. Hence Huangmei sealed the mind with it. Our Sixth Patriarch, on first hearing “let the mind arise without dwelling on anything,” could at once shatter the root of doubt of many kalpas; and when he met Huangmei he could say, “Originally there is not a single thing.” This is the first model of entering by this sutra. So this sutra is the essential formula of the Chan school; students generally regard it as letters, and therefore few know it. Alas for the last age: the true eye is hard to meet, and today it seems harder still. The sutra says that those who read, recite, uphold and copy it have planted good roots not before one Buddha, two, three, four or five Buddhas, but before measureless thousands of myriads of Buddhas. From this we see that even believing, accepting and copying is no shallow causal condition. The novice Fangjue of Caoxi has pricked his blood to write out this scroll, wishing to uphold it all his life. He burned incense, bowed and asked me for a colophon. Moved, I said: A thousand years since the Sixth Patriarch entered cessation, and the Caoxi teaching ground has become a den of foxes; even those who leave home have become woodcutters and cowherds. I came and strove to rescue it from its ills, laboring ten years, restoring and exalting the monastery until it was gradually presentable; then Māra monks wrought mischief and destroyed it from within, and people said the Buddhas and patriarchs had no power, and even I could not explain it away. Now seeing the novice Fangjue able to write this sutra in blood, my heart melts and the ice dissolves. Why? Because the sutra says that if a man adorned buddha-lands as numerous as the Ganges’ sands with the seven treasures, it would not equal upholding a single four-line verse of this sutra, since such conditioned merit must in the end decay, while the surpassing benefit of the unconditioned does not; and because this prajñā is the true seed of Buddhahood. The Buddha said that if one man could be made to arouse the bodhi mind, he would rather his own body suffer the pains of hell — because faith is hard to arouse. Now that the novice Jue alone can take prajñā as his mind, this is truly the fruit of my ten years of toil. Why then should one weigh the restoring of conditioned merit, or hold thoughts of success and ruin? Touched by this, I have written it all down.
Inscribed on Chan Monk Sanfeng’s Lotus Sutra Written in Blood

Beings are deluded as to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, wander far into the five paths and circle through the evil destinies — it is long since this began. The Honored Śākya appeared in the world precisely to reveal and point it out, to enable them to awaken and enter, to rouse in them the will to return, just as a loving father thinks of his son and hopes to hand over the family estate. Therefore he spoke this sutra, to let people quickly reach their old home. Once an old worthy hung the seven scrolls of the Lotus Sutra from a beam. When someone asked him about it, he answered, “These are letters from home.” The monk Sanfeng of Changshu has written out this sutra in his own blood. Is he not one who, seeing a letter from home, longs to return? Truly, this illusory, empty body is the dharmakāya, and in this sutra the Tathāgata’s whole body is already present. Writing it in blood is like a true son in the world identifying his own father: blood dropped on dry bones will surely be seen to seep in. Then is the paper the dry bones of the dharma-body? I therefore append a verse. Lightly I left my native land, not knowing the years; one sheet of letter from home is sent for me alone. Biting my finger, suddenly the heart aches — longing to return, all night I cannot sleep.
Inscribed After Chan Monk Gongquan’s Lotus Sutra Written in Blood

Our original teacher, the monk, from the time of the Buddha Great Unhindered Wisdom Victor, when he was one of the sixteen princes, taught and expounded this sutra and thereby sowed the seed of the One Vehicle’s Buddhahood. Yet those who heard it, deluded, sank through dust-mote kalpas, wandering in birth and death, until on this day at the Vulture Peak assembly they at last awakened and entered, and each received a prediction of future Buddhahood. This is the final, ultimate discourse of the teaching of a whole age. It is like the poor son who long fled to other lands and now first returns to see his father; hearts trust in substance, and he is fit to bear the family estate. This sutra is very like the elder’s written charge handing over the household. Hence it is said that none who hear the Dharma fails to become a Buddha. Therefore Tiantai singles out the five kinds of Dharma masters: those who uphold, read, recite and copy it are all true seeds of Buddhahood. For once one awakens to this mind, whatever flows from the true is true practice, and cannot be compared with what deluded thought holds together. Now the Chan monk Gongquan has roused the unsurpassed mind and written this sutra in his blood, so that the blood of this illusory body drips into the ocean of the Dharma nature and becomes one taste, adorning the fruit of Vairocana’s dharmakāya. He has further vowed to copy the great Avatamsaka Sutra as his ultimate adornment — like the poor son who, having received the written charge of the estate, then reads through the records in the treasury and seeks according to the map. Thus the measureless wonderful adornment of the Avatamsaka world is the great inheritance the Chan monk possesses by nature. Is this not the ultimate one great causal matter? The Chan monk brought the sutra he had written, set out his original vow and asked the old man for instruction; so I have told the whole story from beginning to end.
Colophon to the Brahma Net Sutra Written in Blood

The Brahma Net Sutra is the first proclamation issued by our Dharma King in response to the times, and the precepts it sets out are all precepts of the nature. Therefore in the whole canon, from ordinary being to sage, every stage passed through is established on the diamond mind; and this precept is what is called the diamond mind, truly the great root of Buddhahood. I reflect that we have met this last age, far in time from the sages. If one wishes to escape birth and death and realize the eternal, nothing but this precept suffices to realize it; yet this precept, without the diamond mind, cannot be upheld. The reason all beings sink long in birth and death and cannot get out is precisely their attachment to self; because the view of self is heavy, all karma is committed together, and karma once made, suffering follows it as echo follows sound and shadow follows form — by principle it cannot be escaped. Therefore the essential gate of practice, whether of the greater or lesser three vehicles, takes the breaking of self as root: when self is empty, karma has nothing to bind. Yet the instrument for breaking self, without the diamond mind, is quite simply hard to come by. Examining the Buddha’s intent: since the precept is the pure mind of the self-nature itself, what keeping or breaking can there be? Only, being deluded, it is covered by illusory aggregates and veiled by the dust of feeling, and so it must be lifted off and cleared away. This precept is the sharp weapon that splits the net of views and must be applied at the very first wound; and the beginner bodhisattva, even with sharp faculties and keen wisdom, must take it as his first ground. The student Zhenzhao, by deep former habit of prajñā, willingly left home and studied for years under my Dharma brother Xuelang. He came to see me at Nārāyaṇa Cave just as I was grieving that in the last age few attend to the root. I was reciting the Brahma Net precepts for my disciples, and Zhao heard them and was moved; he begged tearfully to receive the precepts and made a deep and weighty vow, pricking the blood of his tongue to write out this sutra, resolved to uphold it to the end of his life. I was deeply moved and said: Our original teacher Vairocana, from first arousing the mind until Buddhahood, advanced without retreat, giving in charity bodies and lives beyond number, flaying skin for paper, splitting bone for a brush, pricking blood for ink, copying the scriptures until they piled up like Sumeru — because he esteemed the Dharma he did not spare body or life. If you know that birth and death are hard to escape, the root of love hard to cut and the Buddha-fruit hard to await, then practice as the Buddha practiced and vow as the Buddha vowed — what fear is there of not becoming a Buddha? From now on, life after life, writing this sutra in the blood of this body, you should fill a great chiliocosm, and not merely a pile the height and breadth of Sumeru. And those who see, hear and rejoice, who rouse the mind and study it, should be like beans and grain spread over lands in the ten directions — how much more than this single assembly, single man, single crowd? You should exert yourself. I write this especially to attest your vow, and I vow further that this sutra, to the end of future time, may everywhere manifest a body like Many Treasures. Keep it in mind.
Prefatory Note on the Re-engraved Avatamsaka Sutra

The Old Man Vairocana, sitting cold and unable to bear it within a single dust-mote, under a clear blue sky suddenly dozed off and fell into the dream of condition-born deluded thought, stirring up the dust of feeling from kalpas past and all the illusory net-realms of the inexhaustible treasury of great radiant light, layer upon layer interlaced like strings of pearls across heaven and earth, mirroring one another’s images, brilliantly distinct. And he himself gave rise to a great sense of wonder, and was astonished. He announced it to all gods and men of the ten directions, making the tenfold void his mouth and the great earth his long tongue, telling the things of the dream, so that all who heard stared at one another: those with eyes were blind, those with ears were deaf. The great beings on the grounds, priding themselves on being the eldest sons of the house, walked in it themselves and found not one thing — utterly unobtainable; and passing the word to others they could only say it was like the track of a bird in the sky. The Chan monk then vowed, from the tip of a single hair, to let people suddenly enter therein — that too is hard. And yet of all beings on the great earth there is not one who is not buried within this single dust-mote. It only needs a man of great wisdom to let the cold eye bloom: deluded thought is just so, just so. All the various wonderful adornments are present in the net of beings’ daily deluded thought; all the various lights appear at once at every moment, and each uses them daily without knowing it. The reason they do not know is simply that the dream is not yet broken. Now, in the thickets beside the road, one man suddenly leaps up, bares his arms and shouts aloud, and at once the worlds of the ten directions shake in six ways; and all at the same time say to one another in wonder, “How strange, how strange! We did not know that such a rare thing was indeed here.” Then they split it open and come out, and all join hands and play together, free and unobstructed, seeking nothing, and in the end not knowing whose power it was. Those who know the grace should prize it.
Colophon to the Text of the Bodhi Vow

All sages and ordinary beings fundamentally dwell in the diamond mind-ground and are complete in the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom; only by the power of habit perfuming, rousing and transforming do they come to maturity. Therefore in the eight-consciousness field of each being the seeds of the ten dharma realms are present, and they merely sprout according to conditions, so that earlier and later, slow and swift, differ. The Avatamsaka Sutra says that bodhisattvas have ten kinds of habit: the habit of seeing the Buddha, the habit of being born in pure worlds, the habit of practice, the habit of vows, the habit of the pāramitās, the habit of contemplating the equal Dharma, and the habit of various differentiated realms. If bodhisattvas abide in this Dharma they forever leave all habits of affliction and attain the Tathāgata’s great wisdom — the habit that is no habit, and its wisdom. So we know that the two karmas of defilement and purity and the two doors of rising and sinking all arise from perfuming, and are not obtained without cause. Hence the Buddhas, patriarchs and good teachers of old, in teaching people, originally have no real dharma to give and no dharma to transmit or confer; with any who draw near they only observe the thickness or thinness of his defiled and pure habits and tame him according to his illness. They only take on toil and hardship for twenty or thirty years, teaching by word and ear, with morning and evening attendance, even to every kind of hardship and humiliation and a thousand forms of opposition and compliance; all their arrangements are nothing but using the light of great prajñā to steam and perfume the karmic habits of ignorance, to turn defilement into purity and make him know for himself what he originally has. If he can know for himself his originally possessed light of wisdom and let it perfume him from within, growing daily and flourishing monthly, then one day it is like a great blazing fire, and the affliction-habits of before are singed away like a flake of snow on a red-hot stove. Then in daily life, in every encounter and every condition, all is the working of great wisdom; this is what is meant by turning defiled karmic habit into the habit of prajñā-wisdom. If one turns it wholly pure and goes to the very source, and it is no different from where the Buddhas and patriarchs of the ten directions turn, then one simply seals it, saying, “Just so, just so.” That is all; could there be another dharma besides this? Seen thus, the three worthy and ten sagely stages from of old can all turn it but not exhaust it; therefore the ten habits arising from prajñā are the diamond seed, by which, kalpa after kalpa and life after life, ignorance is perfumed and transformed, not stopping until it is pure, till at last one breaks through the skin and comes out. This is why the World-Honored Vairocana gave weight to vow and practice. Dezong first set out from Pu and, following his Dharma kinsman Master Miaofeng, came to serve the old man at Qingliang and then at the seaside — nearly twenty years now. The hardships he has passed through cannot be told in full, yet his earnest, sincere mind for the Dharma has never slackened for a single thought; the old man has only illumined him with the torch of inconceivable wisdom, and has never once opened his lips about the matter beyond, waiting until he believed and acknowledged it himself, so that he would not betray his own spirit. For years he asked the old man, by his own vow, to expound it for him, and the old man would not at first consent. On a winter day of the jiawu year, attending the old man at the Great Cishou Monastery in the capital, he asked instruction on a snowy night and, weeping, told his vow; the old man wrote this out at random for him. In the second month of the following spring the old man, through the cause of spreading the Dharma, incurred the anger of the sage emperor, and the matter reached him as well, and he truly escaped death by a hair. I was exiled to Leiyang; Zong again came ten thousand li from Pu to seek the old man amid the miasmal seas, and meeting him at Wuyang he brought out this scroll. The old man unrolled it and saw its light dazzle the eye, and so appended this.
Prefatory Note on the Chapter of Samantabhadra’s Vows

The Tathāgata Vairocana, dwelling in the Avatamsaka realm, in the bodhi site, expounded the Avatamsaka Sutra for bodhisattvas on the grounds: its verses are as many as dust-motes of three thousand great chiliocosms, its chapters as many as dust-motes of one four-continent world. Even the Great Being Nāgārjuna, with all supramundane wisdom, could not count its chapter titles; and this chapter is the briefest of the brief. The surpassing adornment of the Avatamsaka world, felt as the fruit of the vast causal practices our Vairocana cultivated through distant kalpas, rests in its causal ground upon the ten great vows of Samantabhadra; and these vows accord with the mind of the dharma realm, extend to its full measure and embrace all without exception. Therefore they are called the king of vows. And the essence of practice and the swiftness of attaining Buddhahood surpass nothing this. It is said that one thought annihilates measureless evil karma and one thought perfects measureless good roots. It is like the golden wheel-turning king who dreams he has entered the Avīci hell and suffers great and utter pain, with none to pity or save him; terrified and panic-stricken, he runs and shouts madly, wishing to flee and unable. Then one shout, one great effort, and he wakes with a start: the former suffering cannot be found, and the enjoyment ready at hand is in every way complete from the first. This is what is called the dream-illusion Dharma gate, entered by wisdom; it lies only in one’s own mind and does not depend on seeking outside. Hence it is said, when the mind is pure the Buddha land is pure. My disciple Zheng Kuo has aroused the bodhi mind and taken refuge in the Pure Land. I taught him to recite this chapter exclusively; when one day the dream of birth and death is broken, what fear that he will not see the ready enjoyment of the Avatamsaka?
Inscribed After the Chapter on Peaceful Practices

In youth I read the Four Teachings Manual and saw that Great Master Tiantai assigned the five kinds of Dharma masters to the stage of contemplative practice; I privately had doubts. Then I saw those in the Dharma gate who make upholding the sutra their practice reciting the Lotus Sutra by the hundred thousand fascicles, yet when I examined how they disciplined body and held mind, most could not accord with the sutra. So I knew how hard it is to uphold a sutra. When I composed the Comprehensive Discussion of the Lotus Sutra and came to the Buddha’s praise of the Dharma master’s merit — that one who makes offerings to him gains merit greater than offering to a Buddha, and one who slanders him incurs guilt heavier than slandering a Buddha — this is the golden speech of our World-Honored One. And I saw that the Dharma master who upholds the sutra, in this present fleshly body born of father and mother, obtains purity of the six senses. Now purity of the six senses belongs to the seventh stage of faith, where the bodhisattva is irreversible and never again falls back into birth and death. How can the merit of upholding a sutra reach so far? So we know that upholding lies not in paper, ink and letters but in wondrously matching the Buddha’s mind beyond words; and since the Buddha’s wisdom-life is thereby continued without interruption, its merit is rightly so surpassing. A certain person upholds this sutra and has found an entry in the chapter on peaceful practices, and so upholds it exclusively. This is the World-Honored One’s first and wondrous practice taught to sutra-upholding disciples in the last age; it is the Tathāgata’s own family custom. Entering the Lotus samādhi from here and awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is surely not hard.
Inscribed After the Printing of the Medicine Buddha Sutra

The sutra takes the name Medicine Buddha because it is named after the original Buddha. The utmost sage has no name, but is named by his virtue; and since the Buddha is the king of physicians of the three realms, skilled at healing the mind-illness of all beings, he is called physician. Thus the whole canon is the wondrous medicine suited to the illness, while the illness of beings has delusion and craving as its root. If the root of the illness is not removed, can one wish to escape birth and death and cross the sea of suffering? Question: The sutra says that one who seeks office obtains office, who seeks sons or daughters obtains them, who seeks long life obtains long life, who seeks peace and happiness obtains them. All of these are the deluded craving of beings, and the Buddha’s intent was that beings should leave them; yet if one seeks and always obtains, does this not increase deluded craving? Answer: It does not increase them; it truly wishes to have them left. Because beings do not believe that their own mind is Buddha, they go astray on inverted paths and drown in the river of craving. The Buddha, with vast compassion, pulls them out; since they cannot come out at once, he sets up skilful means to draw and gather them, enticing them onward by what they love — what is called driving out a wedge with a wedge, attacking poison with poison. Hence it is said: first draw them with the hook of desire, then lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom; and so the cravings of the world may be quietly dissolved and silently transformed. Beings begin with the delusion of not believing their own mind: like a man greedy for wealth who dreams of gold and jewels, gives rise to great joy and great delight in desire — yet do gold, jewels and delight come from outside? Beings dwell in this dream-house with every kind of seeking, and the Buddha tames them by the dream-illusion Dharma gate. The heavier the deluded craving, the more extreme the faith in the Buddha; and when faith is extreme, the deluded craving of one’s own mind is transformed into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is again like putting leaven into milk to make cream and butter, which must turn into ghee. This sutra is the Buddha giving beings the medicine of ghee and ambrosia; can one who can take it fail to sweep away a hundred illnesses at once and obtain long life? The layman Liu Qiao has printed this sutra to give to many people, just like an elder giving wondrous medicine at a crossroads. Whoever can believe, accept and take it will have his mind-illness healed at once and obtain whatever he seeks. Is the name Medicine Buddha an empty title? Once one believes in one’s own mind, then this sutra no longer belongs to paper, ink and letters.
Colophon After the White-Robed Dhāraṇī Sutra

The White-Robed Dhāraṇī Sutra flowed forth from the ultimate reality of the great compassion of our Great Being of Perfect Penetration. Therefore good men and women in the world who suffer from having no heir, who hold to it with single-minded hearts, find no prayer unanswered, surely as echo answers sound. Yet those who receive its answer are not few, and those who do not believe are not few, and there are also not a few who hold to it and receive no answer. Why is this? Because our Great Being, relying on his original teacher the Tathāgata Guanyin, was given the illusory diamond samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation, and manifests thirty-two responsive bodies and the merit of the fourteen fearlessnesses, sharing one sorrow and one longing with the beings of the six paths of the three realms of the ten directions. Of the beings of the dharma realm who wish for a son, a son of merit and wisdom is born to them; those born come wrapped in a white robe, as the proof that the Great Being does not deceive beings. And yet, whence does this son really come? If it is the Great Being himself appearing, the Great Being is not deluded — how could every son born be a being of compassionate manifestation? If it is not the Great Being appearing, how is it that by praying to him one obtains a birth? This principle is hard to fathom, and so few believe it. They do not know that the Great Being shares one sorrow and longing with all beings; thus the Great Being’s heart of sorrow and longing is the seeking heart of beings. When the seeker’s heart is truly like the Great Being’s heart, then the Great Being’s heart is also the seeker’s heart — like mirrors exchanging light, each image appearing in the other; like an echo in a valley, sound calling and sound answering. There is no case of one’s own mind not answering one’s own mind. Hence it is said: the own mind grasps the own mind, and what is not illusion becomes an illusory dharma. Thus the son sought is in truth manifested by the seeker’s own mind; because they do not seek in this way, there is no answer. And why is it that when they seek they obtain wisdom and merit? Because ordinary men and women seek purely with a mind of sexual desire, and so mostly get dull-witted children, since these are not born of a mind of wisdom. Now if one does not seek with a mind of desire but seeks from the Great Being, then it springs from wisdom, and wisdom is the root of merit. The son of merit and wisdom so born is what is meant by sound harmonious and echo compliant, form straight and shadow upright; in this principle there is no doubt. Ziyin, the eldest son of the Zhou family, believes firmly in this method; one day he entered the mountain, burned incense, bowed and asked me to write out this sutra. Now I too am one who entered samādhi through the Great Being’s gate of the ear; but I feared that Ziyin could not contemplate in this way, and so after writing it out I have further explained it.
Colophon to Jiang Dayin’s Scroll of a Hundred Cities and Misty Waters

I once read the Life of Qingliang, to the place where Wuzhu entered the Diamond Cave and, over tea with Mañjuśrī, saw great beings drifting down from the clouds. He asked whence these dragons and elephants had come. Mañjuśrī said, “These are the ten thousand members of my household in this cave; each has finished his conditions of benefiting beings in worlds of the ten directions and returned.” He further asked why the world did not know them. Mañjuśrī said, “Some appear as empresses, consorts, princesses and queen mothers of nations; some as ministers, laymen, eunuchs, elders, monks and nuns. They enter according to kind, transforming without end — how can they be measured by their traces?” Now, seeing the holy and compassionate imperial hand grant the eunuch Jiang the scroll of a hundred cities and misty waters, with verses inscribed by the great ministers, one need no longer doubt Mañjuśrī. Lord Jiang, styled Dayin, is an attendant in the Palace of Compassionate Tranquility. In bearing the Tathāgata’s burden, aiding the holy transformation and establishing the Three Jewels, his merit is the greatest; therefore he could obtain this secret seal, no less than the reward of the topknot pearl. He should keep this as his bond for benefiting beings; when one day he returns to the cave, I think Mañjuśrī will see it and find the tallies match.
Colophon to the Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī

All Buddhas alike realize the secret mind-seal and attain unsurpassed bodhi. Held within, it is the secret treasury of the three virtues; uttered, it is the adornment of ten thousand practices; kept, it is the work of benefiting beings; recited, it is the wondrous practice of purifying oneself. Therefore all Buddhas attain the Way through it and all bodhisattvas turn from error through it; thus whatever is called a secret mantra is called supreme and victorious, and this mantra comes from Vairocana’s consecration and was spoken by the dharmakāya — it is the most victorious among the victorious. If it is written on banners, then wherever the wind reaches and the shadow falls, all who are touched can leave suffering and gain happiness; how much more to practice and hold it, to keep it in the heart and make it the mind-seal? Hence the Śūraṅgama says: if beings find the habit of desire hard to remove, they need only with one mind recite my Buddha-crown light-gathering secret spirit-mantra, and the fire of lust is at once removed, like boiling water melting ice, and at the thought it is transformed into unsurpassed awareness. Ah, all beings take sexual desire as the basis of their lives; now if one holds this mantra, the root of life is cut at once and birth and death forever left — how much more shall petty greed, anger, delusion and pride be transformed into the true seed of unsurpassed bodhi? The practitioner Mingkuan has held it for years; now he begs the old man Haiyin to write out this scroll, to wear it all his life, holding and reciting without forgetting. The old man commends his resolve and practice and would strengthen his firmness, so he has written it out and appended this, to spur him on the road ahead and show it to later students.
Colophon to the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings

This Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings: when I formerly lived by the sea I often wrote it out for my disciples to uphold and recite. Since coming here I had forgotten it. Yesterday Master Daguan happened to send me a large-character block-printed edition in the bold hand of the Yuan-dynasty Great Master Xue’an; reading it, I seemed to see an old possession. I have kept it in my box and never taken it out to show anyone. Now the Elder Jingxin of Little Jinshan has happened to bring this volume and asked me to write Dharma words. I was delighted and have written out this sutra once through, and sighed, saying: this suffices to show the meeting of response and the Way, the convergence of time and causal condition. The Buddha taught the Dharma for beings only awaiting the fitness of capacity; hence it is said that he long kept this essential silent and did not hurry to speak, and the reason he had not spoken was that the time for speaking had not come. When I first came to Guangdong I saw no monk deeply devoted to the Buddhadharma. One day, visiting the Elder Jinshan, he brought a volume of the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters copied by various famous gentlemen at his request, and asked me for a colophon. From then on several monks and lay disciples copied the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters. I then expounded it once through for the newly ordained novices under the bodhi tree, and those who heard this sutra were not fewer than a hundred. The capacity was roused by the Elder. This sutra is what gods and men of all worlds rarely hear; all my life I have loved to give this sutra to people, yet in this place alone its capacity did not stir. Now again it has been stirred through the Elder — the affair is strange indeed. Why? Because the Buddha teaches the Dharma only when capacity moves him, and responds only when pressed beyond bearing, like a great bell hung on its frame, sounding according to the strike. So we know this causal matter is not casual. Truly, all beings sleep within this treasury of great radiant light, sunk in the dream of the long night, and have long been unaware. Nothing but great awakening can break the great dream, and nothing but breaking the great dream can warrant being called a great being. Not only is one who can awaken others a great being; one who can strive bravely and awaken himself is also a great being. Thus one must be greatly awake to be a great being, and only a great being can have the great awakening. To break the dream of the endless night with the awakening of a single thought — is that a small matter? Alas, I observe that all beings on the great earth equally possess this awakening and are all great beings; there is only no great being to open and awaken them. Our World-Honored Buddha alone is called the great being. At the Vulture Peak assembly, the outstanding men, and the twirling of the flower and the smile, the wall-gazing at Shaolin, down to the six transmissions and five houses and the seventeen hundred men — all are called those who awaken themselves and awaken others, and are mighty great beings. And all of them were the same as other men. Alas, all beings are certified in perfect enlightenment; the reason they are deluded and do not enter is not that the awakening rejects those who could enter. The point is that in these eight dharmas they cannot awaken; therefore at the critical pass of birth and death they cannot swing their arms free, and so they willingly accept sinking, drive themselves through the bitter destinies, toil and stumble in hardship like hired servants and lowly men, and cannot be called great beings. The Elder could stand out and stir this capacity — is he not like the son of a wealthy house, fallen into a dead-end road, who one day gives rise to the thought of returning home? Now this Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings that I have written is truly a letter brought on a wild goose’s foot; unroll it and you get news of your old home. Try unrolling it from time to time, and do not for a moment forget the plan of return, so that the Compassionate Honored One may not gaze in vain from the land of eternal stillness, leaning at the gate of prajñā.
Colophon to the Records of Śākyamuni and Avalokiteśvara

The learning of the Śākya clan takes the whole substance and great function, exhausting the measure of the dharma realm, as its ultimate standard; this is what is called the power of the majestic spirit of Vairocana’s ocean-seal samādhi, appearing in equality. Therefore the beginning and end of all Buddhas, the work of all bodhisattvas in benefiting beings, and even worldly speech and the crafts of livelihood, all flow from this samādhi and possess vast inconceivable power, complete in the adornments of merit and wisdom; thus one sees the wonder of the dharma realm. And all sages and ordinary beings are included in this. So we know that our patriarch is one man within the samādhi, and the two records of Śākyamuni and Avalokiteśvara he compiled describe the realm of samādhi and turn it into skilful means for benefiting beings; they set out the Dharma gates of the teaching of a whole age, and are again the samādhi within samādhi. How can they be regarded as worldly letters? The wise who look on them — will they not leap into this samādhi? Alas, I am a small man, yet I too have arisen from samādhi to praise them; how can ordinary feeling conjecture about it?
Inscription on the Picture of Universal Nianfo for Rebirth in the Pure Land

Worldly people through kalpas have long sunk in the bitter sea of birth and death, circling in the three evil paths, all because of the deluded thoughts and afflictions of their own minds, committing every kind of karma, and so they have no time of escape. The Buddha taught the one gate of the Western Pure Land to draw and gather beings out of the bitter destinies — the most wondrous Dharma gate, accomplished in a single life. The monk Haihui of Chu urges all in the ten directions who truly work for birth and death to recite the Buddha’s name with one mind and no other condition. Since beings’ afflictions are deep and heavy and their deluded thoughts many, all of them the root of birth and death, nothing but many Buddhas can save the many. I hear that the layman Rudong has printed one image of the welcoming Amitābha Buddha with some eighteen hundred circles over the whole body: for every thousand recitations one fills a circle with red, and when the Buddha’s body is complete, one has recited one million eight hundred thousand times. Though the hundred and eight afflictions of accumulated kalpas are many, relying on the Buddha they are dissolved, the Pure Land may be expected, and the suffering of birth and death forever escaped. And may those urged to recite be as many as the recitations; and may patrons of great faith give paper and print and distribute a like number. When this merit is complete, givers and reciters alike will surely be reborn in Ultimate Bliss.
Inscription on the Appeal for Alms for Huacheng

The great undertaking of printing the canon is, in the more than two thousand years since the Buddhadharma entered China, one great causal matter: it lets measureless beings of the last age plant the true cause of Buddhahood, and even in deep mountains and remote valleys where there is no Buddhadharma all may see the complete canon of the Tathāgata’s great affair. This merit is truly the foremost and rarest excellent work in China. None but one of great compassion and vow-power could arouse this mind; and again none but one of great vow-power could complete the work. It is now past halfway and has already cost tens of thousands; it is not the strength of one man, one hand, one foot. As for the place of cutting the blocks: Wutai was first proposed but suffered from ice and snow; then they moved to Jingshan but suffered from mist and damp — neither was a long-term plan. At last they moved to Huacheng, which may be called the right place. The proposal began with the Hanlin scholar Feng; its restoration was achieved by the Grand Censor Wu; and the one who could carry it was at last found in Master Kai Danju — all of them vow-power beyond measure. But the room storing the blocks must be lofty and broad, with racks to keep them off the ground and let the air through, so that they do not easily spoil. And even when the blocks are done, the work of installing them can hardly be managed by one man’s strength. Now, looking at the appeals of Lords Feng and Wu, who did not even spare head, eyes or marrow, what painstaking hearts were these! I have often said that the men of one generation all share one mind and one former vow, and have long been within the Tathāgata’s treasury of light: it is what is called appearing when the conditions ripen. Now the begging monk is very like one holding an old bond and seeking out those of the same vow; surely those who rise up at first sight were comrades of former days, and are fellows of the same assembly to come. As for what they give, why reckon it in gold and silk? When the mind equals this Dharma in measure, vast as space, the merit too is measured with the realm of space.
Inscription on the Portrait of Master Yunqi

The perfected have no body; they take vow-power as their body. The perfected have no affairs; they take benefiting beings as their affair. Therefore the body is not one’s own and the affair is not done for oneself; thus the body cannot confine them and affairs cannot burden them. Consider that the master dwelt in the world over eighty years and for more than half of it built the work of saving beings; one knows that before he appeared in the world he had already practiced the tools of benefiting others. By his Dharma gate he gathered measureless beings, and of those who together escaped birth and death, who knows how many there were. Thus, though the master came and went with conditions and made an illusion of birth and death, his dharmakāya ever abides, enduring with the mountains and rivers; how can he be sought in this form? Those who look on him should be like Subhūti sitting at ease in the stone chamber, truly seeing the Tathāgata, so that the god-king must scatter flowers and utter praise.
Colophon to the Essay on Releasing Living Beings

The teaching of the sages governs the world by the five constants, with benevolence first; not killing is called benevolence. The Buddha set the five precepts with not killing first. So we know the sages’ minds take compassion as root. The sutra says that filial piety is called the precept; thus the precepts take filial piety as root. For all beings that have awareness possess the Buddha-nature; to kill is to cut off the Buddha-nature, and it is not merely a matter of grudges and debts pursuing one another. Therefore all who are within the long kalpas of birth and death, coming and going through the six paths, have been in every destiny and received every body; so it can be known that the living creatures one kills were in past lives one’s parents, brothers, wives, children and close kin. To kill them now and eat their flesh — is this not flesh and bone devouring one another? The Buddha made filial piety the precept; so we know that not killing is the greatest filial piety, and not merely sparing the lives of creatures. Alas, the delusion of worldly people, accustomed to eating flesh without awakening — is it not grievous? Therefore the sage laid down the precept of not killing to keep the Buddha-nature whole, and this is more than worldly filial piety. This is why Great Master Lianchi universally urged the release of living beings, to receive the Buddha’s mind. If people can follow and practice it, they not only obtain the master’s mind but are fit to fulfill great filial piety, keep the Buddha-nature whole and make the cause of Buddhahood — is that a small matter? Printing this book to broadly transform many people broadens not only the master’s mind but the Buddha’s compassion; it is no ordinary worldly talk. One should believe it firmly.
Inscription on the Record of Immediate Retribution for Killing

The Buddha said that all beings that move and breathe possess the Buddha-nature. He also said that beings, through measureless kalpas, have circled in birth and death and have received a body in every kind. Thus all living things seen now are not only of the same wisdom-life but were close kin in the past, and people are deluded and do not know it. Beings are deluded, and not only eat them: they net profit from others’ lives to support themselves and their parents. What they kill is not only the Buddha’s wisdom-life but their own former kin. It was said before that the retribution comes in a future life; now, looking at this record, the retribution is plainly present before the eyes, seen and heard by all.
