So it is not merely cutting off another’s wisdom-life and killing one’s own former kin; it is killing oneself and hastening one’s own death. Why wait for the future? Should one not fear? Reading this record — as the Buddha said, this is the flower retribution, the fruit lies in hell — if one can keep and practice it, one is practicing the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three times.
Prefatory Note on the Printed Lives of the Five Great Masters

I lately read the Hanlin scholar Qian’s collection of Dharma-protection records and saw the Lives of Eminent Monks at the Founding of the Dynasty by the scholar Song: how magnificent was the flourishing of the Dharma gate! Reverently I think how our Sage Ancestor founded the dynasty, established the Three Jewels and honored the Dharma gate, surpassing a hundred generations, while the famous worthies of the time made the Buddha-patriarchs’ way shine no less than in former days — a moment in a thousand years. From then on it gradually grew still, reaching its lowest at the Jiajing and Longqing periods. What fortune that the late emperor’s holy mother embodied the sage ruler, raising and spreading Buddha-work filling the realm for over forty years without a moment’s rest — something never before seen. As for the dragons and elephants of the Dharma gate, the five great masters met in one age; though their substance and function differ and their principle and phenomena are distinct, in supporting the school and the teachings, opening the eyes of gods and men and making a lamp of wisdom in the long night, they never failed to walk the same road and run in the same track as the Buddhas and patriarchs — how much more, towering and magnificent, as great banners of radiant light! I am fortunate to follow after these masters, though I am ashamed of my own meagerness; I cannot hold up so much as a blade of grass, and can only offer praise, wishing their flowing light not to dim but to illumine the last age. So I have made three inscriptions and two biographies, awaiting those who later keep the monks’ history, that they may gather something from them.
Inscription on the Scroll “The Dharma Thunder Resounds Afar,” Presented to Dharma Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai Preaching in Yunzhong — The Following Are Appended from the Donghai Remains

Before the Buddha appeared and before the patriarch came from the west, when not a dust-mote had been split open, the great earth stood still. All things revealed the body of the dharmakāya and space expounded the wordless sutra; yet those who saw were blind and those who heard were deaf. All were dull in their bright spirit and clear in their karmic consciousness, like one walking on jagged rock in the dark night, or standing naked at a poisonous abyss. The compassionate eye, seeing this, could not bear the grief for them, and leaped up; its shadow fell here, and through ten thousand deaths and one life they shared sweet and bitter together. Earnestly he toiled through the three baskets until his broad, long tongue was parched; shout upon shout, one fist, until his grandmotherly heart bled drops. This is why our master, unable otherwise, came down into the three paths and manifests bodies among other kinds — now stretching like a lion, now turning back like an elephant king — making something out of nothing, turning the false into the true, conjuring gods and men, turning heroes upside down. Thus the gate of ambrosia was opened and the great Dharma thunder shook. At once the cold valley brought forth spring, shoots gradually sprouted, the three grasses and two trees trailed vines and put out branches, and those of high, middle and low faculties whose flowers and fruits ripened cannot be counted. Even his arrangements according to conditions, the knocking and singing done together and the beat made into a command, are nothing but fitting the means to the capacity, driving out a wedge with a wedge; how could there be a real dharma given to anyone? Those who watch the show afterwards take the untrue for true and cling to what is said as unsaid, so that tongue too is parched and heart too bleeds. Alas, the teacher instructs earnestly and the hearer is blank; he leans on it as the true lord, would claim the whole merit, and in the end gets not an inch of reward, and is bound for long kalpas. Why? Because he too makes something out of nothing and turns the false into the true, not knowing that gods and men are conjured, and so brings heroes to be turned upside down. Ghee or poison — birth and death depend on whom? At this I never fail to shed tears. Alas, who can take our master’s mind as teacher? Who can practice our master’s practice? One who follows the master is called a loving father’s filial son; one who can practice it is called the Dharma King’s loyal minister. To love one’s kin and honor the honored — this I have wrung my wrists seeking all my life, and it is hard to find such a man. Only Dharma Master Cheng is such a man. He early paid homage to the King of Emptiness and did not indulge in human falsity; grown, he rose above all existence, strict and pure in the Vinaya — graceful in a turbid world, upright as a green lotus, still in the empty mountains, craggy as ice and snow; his breast full of liver and gall cast in wrought iron, the subtle words of the three baskets strung on a single thread. He is a friend of Mañjuśrī, and so lingers in Mañjuśrī’s ground; he takes the lion as his child, and so plays in the lion’s cave. He brews the cloud of compassion in the empty valley and lets dense mist hang at Qingliang. Now the reed-ash flies and the flower that does not sprout blooms; we shall see spring return to the great earth and joyfully watch all plants flourish. The Dharma thunder shakes in the clouds, ambrosia sprinkles beyond the kalpas, a green lotus is breathed from the tongue-root, ghee irrigates the mind-ground, so that the blind see, the deaf hear, the dull wake, the dead live, the flowering bear fruit and the withered flourish — without self-reliance, without self-praise, neither grasping nor startling, holding the diamond sword, seated in the city of nirvāṇa, so that all the hosts of Māra bow their heads and surrender their lives. Why? Truly because he takes our master’s mind as teacher and practices our master’s practice, knowing how to make something out of nothing and understanding how to turn the false into the true; therefore he too can turn heroes upside down and conjure gods and men. Let him hope to receive the reward of the sewn-in pearl and to loose the bond of long kalpas; he may be called the loving father’s filial son and the Dharma King’s loyal minister. Only thus can he repay our master’s grace and, arm in arm with him, roam in the unborn and undying. Otherwise one only hears his voice and does not see his form — how then is he called a mighty great being? If not so, let him listen to the sound of the clearing of throats of the Buddhas of the ten directions in space.
Inscription on the Scroll of Pilgrimages by Eminent Monks of Our Dynasty, Presented to Elder Huian Jian

The men of old, because the matter of birth and death is great, cut off affection and cast away honor, climbed mountains and forded rivers, consulted teachers and sought one another on the shores of suffering, emptiness and solitude, to decide their own portion and make clear the matter beyond. Often before a man with clear eyes, a lift of the brow or a blink, beneath one staff or one shout, they would suddenly burst apart, body and mind fall away, like a bean popping in cold ashes, so that the root of feeling in birth and death from measureless kalpas was at once pulled out, and they were like a lion cut from its rope, leaping and bounding at will, playing freely with not a hair’s obstruction. Therefore they are called men of great strength. This is the first step of the road for us who have left home, when we set out to surpass the ordinary. Since the first patriarch came from the west he first issued this command, awesome throughout the world: in the Tang, Mazu, Nanyue, Linji, Deshan, Zhaozhou and Yunmen; in the Song, Yongming and Dahui; in the Yuan, Xueyan and Zhongfeng — these elders transmitted a single pulse, like generals beyond the gate of the capital, their wind traveling ten thousand li. Therefore whoever met the hammer and tongs and fell into that poisonous hand was wholly shattered, bones and flesh dissolved together. Alas, the sages are far off in time and this way is desolate; those who understand the tone are few. In our own dynasty it is blankly unheard of, and I am sick at heart over it, thinking the lion’s string had fallen silent. Begging in the royal city, I dwelt illusorily in the Maitreya Pavilion, and one day the layman Yan brought eighteen verses for monks setting out on pilgrimage by the venerable elders of the founding of the dynasty. Reading a few words from the abbot’s hall of Great Master Jitan Le, I found his style and rule quite sufficient, no less than the ancients. I rejoiced and praised: what fortune, in these two hundred years and in this last age, to see the vast samādhi of the earlier awakened on the tip of a single hair — truly a former bond. This scroll has already been presented to the secret treasury; I therefore add a few words, wishing to spread these sayings among men. It happened that the three Hanlin scholars Tang Yisuo, Yuan Yupan and Wang Zhongbai came to call and spoke of wishing to compile a Life of Eminent Monks of our dynasty, gathering widely the pilgrimage records of the Dharma gate; so I entrusted this to them. Then Elder Huian Jian saw it and earnestly asked for it. He entered the yellow gate in youth, amid brocade and jade, yet his will grieved over birth and death and one day he cast it all off like spittle, traveled far to famous mountains, consulted teachers and sought widely for decision. Now he hides at Funiu; I think he must have met that poisonous hand like the ancients, and so finds these words close to him. Otherwise they would be like chewing a soup of wood shavings or biting an iron meal. He is about to return to his old mountain and I too shall go back east to my cave; sparing no fatigue, I have written it out once. If he can see the ancients clearly through this one word, only then will he not betray the will to leave home and can stand as a model beyond the dust. Otherwise he not only fails to prize his own spirit but drags Haiyin down with him.
Inscribed After Master Zhulin’s Dharma Words to His Student Zhenzong

Those who take Chan as their school mostly disparage the teachings, and those who study the teachings are mostly blind to Chan; thus Chan and the teachings are made into two separate stakes. The masters of old could not after all unify their purport; even Guishan, who harmonized the school and the teachings, was still said to be seeing the moon through gauze. For a thousand years up and down, students have been unable to unify their direction. There is no other reason: they lack a clear-eyed transmission from a teacher to break down the hedge for them. As it is said, it is not that there is no Chan, only that there is no teacher. Because the Chan school lacks wide learning and the teaching school lacks the true eye, this great Way is hard to make clear. Great Master Zhulin of Qingliang sat on the flower seat with ten thousand fingers around him, skilled at expounding the essentials of Dharma, called the doctrinal dragon of his day; yet his daily conduct did not stray onto mysterious paths. Looking at the words he showed his students, they have much of the Chan school’s manner. Without the true eye, how could his words and breath be so powerful and robust? Can he be summed up as a master of letters? Alas, students have long fallen into the net of knowledge and views, and nothing but the diamond king’s sword can split it with one stroke. In showing this to the student Zhenzong, the master surely took him for a plant of the household; he will certainly not betray this one causal matter. If one regards it as ordinary tangled vine, one not only misses it face to face but betrays the grace of Dharma deeply.
Inscribed After the Pilgrimage Scroll of Attendant Sanshan Zhen

These are the words of eighteen eminent monks at the founding of the dynasty, shown to pilgrim monks. I privately hold that the single pulse of the Chan source, after Zhongfeng, was silent and without men; from Konggu onward it mostly carried a fine fastidiousness, and no longer had the ancients’ manner, like a lion slipped from its rope. In the winter of the jiawu year I lodged in the abbot’s quarters of Cishou in the great capital, and Lord Yan Xiyun brought me the verses he had recorded. I read them three times and sighed: the eye of gods and men is still undestroyed. Pity that I could not see the old men’s own hand. I noted them down and kept them. In the third month of the next year I met with disaster through the Dharma and was sent to Leiyang. I left the capital in the tenth month of that year. My attendant Fushan gathered my Haiyin drafts, carried the book-box and crossed the ranges with me; in the intervals of travel he came and went between the miasmal seas and Caoxi for fifteen years. In the first month of spring of the gengxu year I was glad to lay down the burden of Caoxi and my body was free; Shan wished to return home to visit his family. Five days after the Lantern Festival, carrying my accumulated drafts of several years, he sorted the worn papers in the boat on the Meng River, and by chance found this scroll and read it. I recalled with emotion how the ink of that day’s inscription was not yet dry when I set out on a journey of ten thousand li — who would have thought I would suddenly come upon this old thing today? The ancients said: to know the meaning of the Buddha-nature, observe the causal conditions of time and season. Is this not the hidden blessing of the Buddhas and patriarchs, embracing him with spiritual power? Otherwise, why should he see this at both beginning and end, as if emerging from the square-net samādhi at the snap of a finger and the clearing of a throat? Unrolling the scroll by lamplight, I was so glad I could not sleep. So I wrote it out again for my attendant. Alas, I am old and decayed and hardly fit to walk arm in arm with those elders; Shan should be no less than the attendant Zhen of Sanshan in the matter of pilgrimage. When the ancients casually let fall a word or half a phrase it covers all like heaven and holds all like earth; this old man’s picking it up at random and doing great Buddha-work on the tip of a hair makes the elders seem to be stopping their ears while stealing a bell, and this old fellow cannot avoid adding feet to a snake. Let the attendant Shan tie it in a bundle and throw it into the great ocean of the east — that would be a hundred paces ahead of Sanshan. Otherwise he will not have finished with his ancestors, and the calamity will reach his sons and grandsons.
Inscribed After Chan Master Daguan’s Scroll for Three Chan Monks Setting Out on Pilgrimage

From of old those who leave home, because they cannot decide the great matter of birth and death for themselves, prepare straw sandals, climb mountains and ford rivers, and seek out great teachers to decide it. But the great good teacher is like a lion crouched on the ground: not a hair dares brush against him; brush against him and the root of life is cut at once. When he lets fall a word or half a phrase, it is like thunder and lightning in a clear sky, leaving one deaf and dazzled, with no time to save one’s own life — how much less to dare toy with Buddhadharma and the Chan way? The gain and loss in this are known to few. Alas, in two hundred years there have been no few pilgrim monks; how many have offended against this command? Now these three Chan monks take pride in their pilgrimage, and their resolve is commendable. Having seen Chan Master Daguan, his claws and fangs are already revealed, yet their root of life is not cut, and they wish to seek other teachers. Seeing this scroll I laughed and said: these three Chan monks carrying this scroll on pilgrimage are like requesting the imperial sword to put down rebels — I wonder how they will report back in days to come.
Inscribed After Master Daguan’s Funeral Address for the Great Monk Bianrong

Long ago Ji of Yanling hung his sword at the tomb of the prince of Xu, saying he had promised it in his heart while the man lived and repaid the knowing after his death; this was held to be a righteousness high above a thousand ages. If worldly truth is so, how much more the supramundane? The men of old, because the matter of birth and death is great, cut off affection and took leave of kin, consulted teachers and decided it. Whenever a single word opened them, the giver was like heaven covering all and the receiver like earth upholding all; they matched in the space of a flint-spark and lightning-flash, and the dust of feeling in birth and death burst apart like thunder. Was that an accident? Therefore the grace is deep, like a drop entering the sea, to dry up only with it — how could it be limited to before and after death? Reading Master Da’s funeral address for old Bian, I am deeply moved. Ah, a single meal repaid with a thousand in gold is thought a wonder, yet one word that does not fade through the exhaustion of kalpas — how is that ordinary? Alas, old Bian saved beings for over sixty years, and his Dharma gift nearly filled the earth; as for knowing grace and repaying grace, how few in the world! If everyone were like Master Da, then the causal ground of Great Unhindered Wisdom would not need to be sought in the ink-kalpas before. And what makes old Bian undying rests on one word; what makes that one word undying rests in these dots of ink. If the reader is like this, he may be called not betraying his original possession.
Colophon to the Song of the Buddha’s Slave

The young monk Dachuan of Wu roused a great mind and vowed to feed one hundred and eight thousand people with a single bowl; his practice is the most arduous. Therefore the elders and laymen, hearing of it, were glad and all praised him. Only Gu Shifu’s song has the line about the Liang emperor begging to be a slave of the Buddha’s house, marking how he can forget his body for the Three Jewels and thereby shaming a little all in the world who so prize themselves that they are not even equal to the Liang emperor. Chan Master Daguan Ke saw it and thought it remarkable; he did his utmost to portray the slave and made it into a song to bring it out. I sang it long in three refrains and sighed: even if the yellow-faced one and the blue-eyed one met this, they would hold their bellies and fall over laughing — how much more the slavish slave? As for the matter beyond in the Chan school, it does not touch mysterious paths and is peerlessly noble; yet even to dwell in that nobility is still to be a slave boy or serving girl, called a fall from the summit — how much more all the various thoughts and clingings flowing out into the formations? And yet, how does the young monk come to be in this position? I often recall a rich master who was hard to please and had one slave after his own heart. By day the master indulged every wish in ordering the slave about, and the slave suffered without ever satisfying him; by night the master dreamed he was the slave and the slave dreamed he was the master, and again indulged every wish in ordering the slave about, and the slave again could not satisfy him. Yet dream and waking are equal while pain and pleasure differ — what wonder is there in that? Now this monk would take the slave of the daylight and seek to be the master of the dream. And the hundred and eight thousand he feeds — are they not also masters of the daylight who will become slaves in the dream? Ah, birth and death and nirvāṇa are like yesterday’s dream. If the monk knows this, he can with a drop of water make offerings to the Buddhas and beings of worlds as numerous as the Ganges’ sands in the ten directions, with inexhaustible enjoyment. Why fuss over one hundred and eight thousand? Let him not with a measuring mind cut himself off from the Tathāgata’s measureless realm.
Prefatory Note on the Shouchang Recorded Sayings

The old man of Shouchang, in the conduct of his whole life, only cast off body and life on the shores of empty mountains and solitude, tilling the soil and winning a bellyful of breath; and in daily life he splashed it out before the assemblies of gods and men like beating a poison drum, so that those who heard the sound went deaf and those poisoned died. And how many were poisoned? I recall how the yellow-faced old one, at the Vulture Peak assembly, led a band of muddled fellows who day by day put on their robes and took their bowls, went along the streets and through the lanes, begged a handful of cold rice, and coming back ate their fill, washed the bowls, put away the robes, sat cross-legged and idly tangled vines — taking this as their household living. So it went for over thirty years while the assembly of gods and men looked on blankly, never knowing what it was all for. Then one day Subhūti saw through it and sighed aloud: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The World-Honored One, seeing the movement and stillness of his eyes, then did his utmost and made a muddled assault, until Subhūti’s slightest doubt was utterly cleansed and his root of life cut off. So Subhūti, moved to the heart, wept tears and cried aloud, wept and praised, unable to keep silent. Only then did the yellow-faced old one’s stifled feeling find a little ease, and he was no longer unfaithful to his former piece of grandmotherly kindness. Now, looking at Shouchang’s hoe, it is very like the yellow-faced one’s robe and bowl, and these words are no less than the Vulture Peak’s tangled vines. One should know that when these words spread widely they are like the sound of the poison drum; who knows how many will be poisoned by them — and of those who are moved to tears like Subhūti, who knows how many there can be? A proverb says: acquaintances fill the world, but how many know the heart? Those who read these words later — if they take them as a matter of words, they fail Shouchang; if they do not take them as a matter of words, they fail themselves. If they would fail neither, they must, before the hoe is lifted, at the very place where he grips it, take it up for themselves.
Colophon to Chan Monk Ke’s Pilgrimage Scroll

Long ago Fazhao, at his meal, saw ten thousand Buddhas and bodhisattvas appear in his bowl and did not know why; he asked a monk, who said, “This is the transformation realm of Mañjuśrī at Mount Wutai.” So he set out and walked to Mount Wutai, wishing to see Mañjuśrī, and indeed at last saw Mañjuśrī, who gave him the Dharma gate of reciting the Buddha’s name. The Chan monk Zhaoke has first obtained the nianfo samādhi from Yunqi; it is well that he now wishes to go and seek Mañjuśrī’s confirmation. But if he asks about the Dharma assembly of the south, he must not let the three-before and three-after deceive him to his face.

The Chan monk Zhaoke first lived on Mount Huang and took the Avatamsaka as his work — what is called entering right samādhi within a single dust-mote. Now, from the place where he rises in another quarter, he wishes to break the dust-mote and bring out the sutra, and will cut thatch by the West Lake. He thinks he needs the elder to plant a blade of grass; this old man simply says no. In the unobstructed dharma realm, whatever condition one meets is the school, and everything is complete wherever one is; one need only be clear within one’s own mind — why borrow from outside?
Dream Wanderings of Elder Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Two
Inscribed at the Head of the Platform Sutra for Chan Monk Zhijing

The Buddhas and patriarchs from of old appeared in the world for the great matter of birth and death, and none failed to give up body and life, passing through every hardship and coming out of ten thousand deaths into one life. Consider our original teacher, the old man Śākyamuni: through vast kalpas, for the sake of this Dharma, he gave up heads, eyes and marrow more than the Ganges’ sands; and when he finally emerged, he still endured six years of cold and hunger in the Snow Mountains, and then horse-fodder and the golden spear-wound — nothing did he not accept. And all he barely won was the breath of rice-gruel over forty-nine years, with nothing extraordinary to show. And at the last he stirred up a laughing matter that spreads through the world to this day. Then he sent the blue-eyed one to come especially from the west, who took it as a real thing and tricked Shenguang into losing an arm by mistake; and when it came to old Lu, the rustic fellow, one phrase teased him and thrust him into the black lacquer bucket, and those who were stifled to death number more than ten thousand times ten thousand. From the night at Huangmei when he laid down the stone at his waist and picked up a few scraps of worn rope, taking them for a rare treasure — who would have thought that they would drag men to death by ten thousand times ten thousand more? And happily, having leaped out of the thicket of the hunt, full of shame, he would often tell people of the places where he had stumbled in his life; even with the great void for a mouth he could not bring out a single bit of it, so that the handle of the story drifted through the rivers and lakes and those who passed it on again took it for a real thing. How sad! I too, for the sake of this Dharma, incurred imperial anger and truly came out of nine deaths; happily I revived at the dead end, and by grace was exiled to Leiyang. On a winter day of the yiwei year of Wanli I left the imperial capital and went south through the snow, reaching Baixia, where I took with me my disciples Zhijing and Ruguang as my shadow. When we came to Leiyang the miasmal pestilence raged greatly, and of those who drank the water scarcely one in ten thousand was whole. I and my followers all caught the poisonous fever; Guang did not survive, and Jing died twice and came back to life. Had we not relied on the spiritual power of the Buddhas and on our own vows to hold on, not one in ten thousand would have been left. When Jing’s illness eased a little I sent him back to Mount Lu to visit his teacher, and to borrow the light of ten thousand acres of lake and a thousand feet of waterfall to wash away the habit that remained. At parting I had nothing to enjoin him with, and suddenly picked up this scroll from my desk and gave it to him. You will see how the ancients, after the great death, had such news as this — but none but one who has truly died can obtain it. Jing should hold it on the summit of a lone peak, before a cliff of ten thousand fathoms, and try it where his hand can reach; he will surely see. If he can truly give up body and life like the ancients, then he will not only be faithful to what this old man has done today but will not betray the supreme diamond seed he has planted through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives. Exert yourself and do not forget what has been enjoined. Written before the lamp on the night of the nineteenth of the long-day month of the bingshen year of Wanli, in the rampart walls of the eastern quarter of Wuyang.
Prefatory Note on the Outline Sections of the Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra

Dividing a sutra into sections is an ancient practice. Long ago Dharma Master Dao’an divided sutras into three parts, and people of the time mocked him for splitting the sutra’s meaning; but when the treatise of Bandhuprabha arrived, it indeed divided the whole sutra into three parts, and then they sighed at how well it matched. For each sutra has its own guiding principle, and sectioning is a matter of grasping the main points, so that the reader gets the essentials and may, leaving words, obtain the meaning and awaken to it, discarding the trap and snare — it is hardly a matter of chopping into pieces and giving free rein to private judgment. Later students of doctrine, blind to the purport beyond words, each relied on his own view and multiplied redundant theories, incurring the guilt of slandering the Dharma and leaving students with nowhere to turn — what is called losing the sheep because the paths fork too many ways. The Laṅkāvatāra takes the first principle beyond verbal expression as its school. Its text is broad and its meaning deep; the old explanations only sectioned the text without fully grasping the meaning, and the purport that runs through it as one was not made clear, so that readers followed the words and lost the meaning, and those cultivating the three contemplations of mind could find no gate to enter. Though the lectures of past and present have spread through the whole earth, of those who practice accordingly few know the essentials, and they fail the Tathāgata who revealed the right path of practice. Now I have rashly made a comprehensive discussion, wishing simply to set out the thread of the mind so that students may see the guiding purport at a glance. The outline sections first gather the essential meaning to show the purport beyond the text, so that one knows the source of question and answer and fuses it into one, clear to mind and eye, hoping that one may forget the words and obtain the meaning and not be obstructed by phrases. Yet even this is already superfluous. Later students must on no account think it lacking and add theories of their own, bringing on themselves no shallow guilt of slandering the Dharma. On the Buddha’s enlightenment day in the first month of summer of the wuxu year of Wanli, the monk Deqing wrote this among the rampart walls of the Green Gate at Wuyang.
Inscribed After the Commentary on the Diamond Sutra

The Buddha-nature wrapped in affliction is like a pearl in one’s bosom or water in the ground: though it is inherently there, without pointing one does not know it and without digging one does not get it. Thus a good friend and teacher is the one who points to the pearl, and the measureless Dharma gates are only the method of digging — how could they be a real dharma? The Tathāgata appeared in the world for one great causal matter: the revealing, showing, awakening to and entering of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the Buddha-nature of beings, that is, the true wisdom of prajñā. And this true wisdom we possess complete from the first, with no increase or decrease — just like the pearl in the hem of the robe, in itself neither bright nor dim, and the water in the ground, whose source is shallow or deep. Thus the Dharma is neither sudden nor gradual; awakening alone is easy or hard, according to whether faculties are sharp or dull and obstructions thick or thin. One of sharp faculties and keen wisdom, with thin obstructions and thick virtue, understands at a touch — this is easy awakening, and so is called sudden. Our Sixth Patriarch, hearing the single phrase “let the mind arise without dwelling on anything,” awakened at once to what he originally had and so awakened to the unborn. This was because the conditions of prajñā from many kalpas had ripened; touched at the right moment, he was instantly clear and confident, like opening his robe and seeing the pearl, which was his from the first and not sought outside. How easily is such a thing seen? Alas, in man the ground of ignorance is hard and the water of the Dharma nature lies deeper still; while the work of clearing and digging is not yet evident, to seek to ride the current back to the ocean of wisdom is surely hard. Therefore the sage, unable otherwise, set up means: according to the five natures he established the three vehicles, and following sharp and dull faculties he opened sudden and gradual. The discourse of the eight divisions of prajñā is still but the first step of entering the Great Vehicle, and this sutra is only one of the eight; it is called Diamond for its ability to cut. It points directly at one’s own Buddha-nature, firm and indestructible, cutting off ignorance at once, free of all marks, thusness unmoving — just like the pearl in the robe that was never dim; only, the pointing must come from another while the awakening lies with oneself. Thus the sutra is the method of pointing and knowing, and the commentary only the method of digging. As for drinking a drop and gaining coolness, removing the fever of affliction and loosening the thirst of craving, that place where the mind clears and the spirit is released — the drinker alone knows it, and it can hardly be poured out to another. Mr. Su Shuda has borne the prajñā seed from former lives; all his life he has been devoted to this sutra, and moving among the Hanlin scholar Jiao and other great teachers, his confidence has grown firmer. Obtaining this commentary, he felt he had found a priceless treasure and at once had it cut on blocks to spread the Dharma gift widely. Seeing this I rejoiced, joined my palms and praised him: The dragon king Sāgara can with a drop of water rain down and fill the Jambudvīpa, moistening the scorched and withered and bringing the hundred things to life — that is but the transformation of his karmic power. How much more what is perfumed and issued by the wondrous wisdom of prajñā? From this we know that Mr. Su’s merit of Dharma-giving is great.
After Copying the Verses on the Diamond Sutra

The seventeen verses on the Diamond Sutra above were composed in the late autumn of the jiyou year at Baolin in Caoxi while I was lecturing on the Diamond Prajñā for my disciples who had come. I often think how the Sixth Patriarch, hearing a single phrase of this sutra, saw his own mind as clearly as a fruit in his palm and reached the ground of no doubt; therefore from Huangmei onward he sealed the mind by this sutra alone. I had drifted with the waves and not reached the other shore; not knowing where the huatou lands, I took it all for letters, and so it became an obstruction instead. Lately, at the place where Subhūti sighed, “Rare indeed,” I suddenly saw through, and only then believed the ground where the ancients do not deceive: it all arises from the root of doubt in one’s present daily life. At the Vulture Peak assembly the great disciples drew near the Tathāgata day and night without interval for thirty years, yet were as blind and deaf; in the World-Honored One’s daily life, in the lifting of his brows and the blinking of his eyes, in walking, standing, sitting and lying, they did not observe a single hair, and at all his various revelations they fell into the net of doubt. Had Subhūti not seen through it that day, they would have missed it face to face to the end. How much more those in the last age who seek the Way, drawing near teachers and friends — how easily do they believe? The Sixth Patriarch, on first entering Huangmei’s room, believed through and through without doubt. Linji, on first entering Huangbo’s room, took the staff three times, just like the Vulture Peak disciples thirty years before. But after his root of life was cut at Dayu’s place, when he saw Huangbo again he could say, “Only because your grandmotherly heart was so urgent” — this is exactly like Subhūti in that quiet place seeing through the World-Honored One and sighing, “Rare indeed.” Alas, from of old the moment of transmission between teacher and disciple is truly not easy. It is said that only when one’s seeing surpasses the teacher’s is one fit to receive the transmission — like water poured into water, like space meeting space. Watching Subhūti face the World-Honored One, do not say he had no doubt; it is only that at the place where the World-Honored One raised it up he moved like a good horse at the shadow of the whip — a gulf of heaven and abyss from when his eye was not yet open. These verses, as far as Subhūti is concerned, are very like adding feet to a snake. Yet I am glad to show Subhūti’s liver and gall, no different from where Subhūti saw the World-Honored One — like beating time for one who sings of an illusory man. The attendant Shan has served this old man for over twenty years; in raising up this matter in daily life he is no less than Vulture Peak, and in passing through hardship and peril he is far beyond Subhūti. If his mind were not like Subhūti’s seeing, how could he digest all these sorrows? At the time, through Māra’s work, I was confined in a single leaf of a boat on the Furong River; on a cold night I wrote this and gave it to him — very like the shadow of a wild goose in the cold sky.
Colophon to the Treatise on the Non-Movement of Things

In youth I read Sengzhao’s treatises and found no resting place in the purport of non-movement; I was always in doubt over the four lines about the whirlwind and the rest. Later I had an insight, and then believed that Master Zhao had deeply awakened to reality. And reading the great Avatamsaka commentary, at the chapter on asking about understanding — “like the water in a river, rushing and racing away” — Great Master Qingliang quoted Master Zhao’s verse on non-movement to attest it, esteeming his insight as wondrously matching the Buddha’s meaning. I once spoke of this to a friend, and he would not allow it at all; on the contrary he made Master Zhao out to be a one-view heretic and widely cited doctrine to refute him. Even elders of the Dharma gate like Great Master Yunqi Da and others argued with force, yet in the end did not turn his opinion. I read the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, where the monk Fojian addressed the assembly: he cited a monk asking Zhaozhou, “What is the meaning of non-movement?” Zhou made the gesture of flowing water with both hands, and the monk had an insight. Again a monk asked Fayan, “Not grasping at marks, thusness unmoving — how does one not grasp at marks and see the unmoving?” Fayan said, “The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night,” and that monk too had an insight. If one can see it here, then one knows that the whirlwind flattening mountains is originally forever still, and rivers racing along are from the first not flowing. If not, one cannot avoid more chatter: Heaven turns left, earth turns right; from ancient times to now, how many rounds? The golden crow flies, the jade hare runs; scarcely out of the sea gate, it falls behind the green hills. The rivers’ waves stretch far, the Huai and Ji roll on, straight into the blue deep, flowing day and night. Then he raised his voice and said: Chan worthies, do you see thusness unmoving? Now Zhaozhou and Fayan were old generals of the Chan gate, great elders who transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal, and Fojian cited them to expound the purport of non-movement before the assembly, clear as the white sun in the sky — by no means a master who merely keeps doctrine and letters and can be looked at from the cliff’s edge. Can Master Zhao then be taken for a heretic view? I write this to show students, so that regarding the meaning of the non-movement of things they may trust it for themselves beyond words.
Colophon to the Re-engraved Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama Sutra

The Śūraṅgama Sutra is the unsurpassed summit Dharma; its text covers the three baskets and its teaching embraces the five periods. It penetrates the root of delusion and awakening and exhausts the essential road of sage and ordinary being; of true practice and wondrous gates, none surpasses it. Therefore the Chan practitioner who does not enter this Dharma has no clear true eye, and the student of the teachings who does not master this sutra cannot break through the repeated passes. Since it entered China there have indeed been many interpreters, yet the great purport that runs through it has never been brought to completion. Lately there are men of perverse interpretation who even twist mysterious sayings to attach them to outside doctrines and destroy right view, and the world cannot distinguish it; the harm is no small matter. Those who bear the wisdom-life shudder at it. Lately the Elder Yuan of Chuping, long resident in Yuzhang and gathering those with conditions, grieved deeply that the banner of wrong views is hard to pull down; he therefore assembled monks and lay companions and donated the printing of the text in Sanskrit form, to raise the banner of right Dharma, hoping that all wise and aspiring men of the Dharma gate will deeply probe the Buddha’s meaning and not fall into icchantika. Then for the ocean of Dharma this is the ferry and the sail. Is his merit of protecting the Dharma a small supplement? I respectfully write this to lead the chorus.
Prefatory Note on the Printed Straight Explanation of the Awakening of Faith

This treatise is the key and bolt of the Chan school and the great outline of the teachings. He who draws near the teachings cannot know their essentials without it; he who practices Chan cannot open the true eye without it. It is truly the compass of the nature and characteristics schools. Its text is brief and its meaning deep, embracing without omission the one mind of the dharma realm, principle and phenomena, cause and fruit, practice and realization, sudden and gradual. Therefore the student of the Dharma gate who sets it aside and seeks awakening is stepping backward to go forward. The old commentary of Xianshou is precise and thorough, and Changshui’s record is vast and boundless; the shallow-minded wander with no home. I first took the root commentary, omitted its elaborate sections and compiled an outline commentary, which has already been printed and circulated; but thinking it still hard for beginners, I have again used the sense of the commentary to explain directly following the text, valuing coherence and not borrowing side branches, so that the meaning of the one mind, true and false, deluded and awakened, is wholly clear, like distinguishing black from white. In truth I only follow the former intent and dare not overstep it; I merely make it easy to grasp following the text, without laborious searching, reaching straight to the source, as a small aid for new students.
Colophon to the Printed Hundred Dharmas Treatise and the Rule of the Eight Consciousnesses

The Hundred Dharmas and the Eight Consciousnesses are the compass of the characteristics school and the gate of entering the Great Vehicle. The Buddha’s teaching of mind-only and consciousness-only pervades the whole canon; Maitreya condensed it to six hundred and sixty, Vasubandhu condensed it to a hundred dharmas, and the hundred fascicles of the Consciousness-Only treatise were condensed by the Tripiṭaka Master to forty-eight lines of verse — one may call it most brief and most essential; it is the net-cord of the dharma realm. Because all beings, deluded as to the one mind, make it into consciousness, and ignorance blinds their present daily life so that they do not know the pivot of good and evil in their own minds. As for the student of the teachings, he opens the scroll and sees only the obstruction of words, not knowing that all that is said is the Buddha-nature inherent in his own mind; and the Chan practitioner hugs deluded thought, practicing and smelting blindly, and never reaches the root of birth and death. Both these are the fault of not knowing this treatise. Yet the treatise is but about five hundred words and the verses only forty-eight lines, and they gather up the whole teaching of one age; worldly and supramundane dharmas are all embraced, and both the teachings and Chan have their right path of practice revealed. The aspiring student spends less than a month’s effort and penetrates it wholly without omission. Alas, the unaspiring cannot give their minds to it and are content to be benighted — is it not sad? Commentators ancient and modern mostly cite the root text of the Consciousness-Only treatise, which beginners find hard to enter, and it is also inconvenient for conventional truth. So I have taken its meaning and changed its wording to suit beginners and make it easy to enter; the text seems lacking but the meaning is in fact complete. This too is teaching in accord with conditions, and I do not presume to damage the established words of the ancient worthies and incur the guilt of slandering the Dharma.
Prefatory Note on Copying the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters

This sutra is the root Dharma wheel turned by our World-Honored Buddha when he first attained right awakening. Its purport takes the one mind as its school, hence it says, “To know the mind and reach the root is to be called a monk.” It takes cutting off desire and leaving the dust as its function, hence it says, “Apart from desire and still — this is foremost.” It also says, “He who cuts off craving is like one whose four limbs are cut.” It takes cream as the mark of its teaching, because ghee comes from milk and cream, and the unsurpassed Buddha-fruit is rooted in the one mind of true and false. Truly the mind is the root of the dharma realm and desire the source of all suffering; now, to leave suffering and gain happiness, cutting off desire is put first. The essentials of practice in the world and beyond it are no other than this; hence it is the root Dharma wheel. Master You said, “Filial piety and fraternal respect — are they not the root of benevolence?” To accord with one’s parents is filial piety and to respect elders is fraternal respect; and our Buddha also said, “Filial piety is called the precept: to be filial and obedient to the Three Jewels, to parents, teachers and monks, and to be filial and obedient to the Dharma of the utmost Way.” Is this not taking accord with the enlightened nature as the root of restoring the nature? Alas, all beings take sexual desire as the basis of their lives and have been confused in it for long. Yet nature and desire are but a dust-mote and a clod of mud; if one is not a bold, fierce man who cuts it off with the diamond mind, can one escape great suffering and attain utmost joy? Confucius said, “If a man has desires, how can he be firm?” Without firmness, one can only gaze at this Dharma gate as at a vast ocean. Therefore our Buddha, appearing in the world, spoke first of this Dharma gate of leaving desire — it is like pricking a needle into the painful spot. Hence the sutra repeatedly and earnestly presses the point. All who study the Buddha’s Way and aspire to clarify this mind, if they set this aside and speak of practice, are stepping backward to go forward.
Inscribed After the Sixteen Sublime Contemplations

The sixteen sublime contemplations began because Queen Vaidehī, afflicted by her rebellious son King Ajātaśatru, begged the Buddha for compassionate rescue. The Buddha therefore came in person to her prison, released a light from between his brows that illumined the buddha-lands of the ten directions, and had the queen choose for herself, to be reborn according to her wish. The queen loved only the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so the World-Honored One spoke these sixteen sublime contemplations especially, as the means of rebirth. If but one contemplation is accomplished, one surely obtains one’s wish. Therefore the one gate of the Pure Land is the most direct road of transcending birth and death, and those past and present who have practiced it and obtained proof cannot be counted. Some suppose it was set up for those of middle and low faculties — not so. With one light the Buddha at once illumined the buddha-lands of the ten directions, clear before the eyes; how could that be the realm of middle and low faculties? And to escape in one life the birth and death of measureless kalpas — how could that be within the power of middle and low faculties? Alas, in the last age people are mostly wild and boastful, giving free rein to mouth and ear to furnish talk; even a man of the highest faculties gains nothing by it. It is said: medicine need not come from Bian Que’s prescription — whatever cures the illness is good. How much more this Dharma gate, personally handed down and verified by the Dharma King, and the wondrous practice already proven by Vaidehī. To set it aside in practice and seek something mysterious is either folly or madness — truly making obstacles for oneself. How sad! We disciples, monks of the Śākya clan, have left the dust in body, yet our mind-source is turbid, racing day and night in the arena of the five desires with never a thought of turning the light back on our own minds; and worse, we talk wildly of prajñā and lightly scorn the Dharma gate, content in our hearts with the hells and never waking — is it not pitiable? A certain disciple asked instruction, and the old man wrote out these verses especially as a support for pure karma, hoping for real practice and real proof, so as not to betray the pilgrimage of leaving home in this life. If one sets aside this Dharma gate and seeks the beyond elsewhere, would the Buddha mislead people? And would Great Master Yongming deceive people?
